Abstract.

We study asymptotics of sums of the form ∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)​Λ​(n+h)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n)\Lambda(n+h), ∑X<n≤2​Xdk​(n)​dl​(n+h)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}d_{k}(n)d_{l}(n+h), ∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)​dk​(n+h)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n)d_{k}(n+h), and ∑nΛ⁡(n)​Λ​(N−n)\sum_{n}\Lambda(n)\Lambda(N-n), where Λ\Lambda is the von Mangoldt function, dkd_{k} is the kthk^{\operatorname{th}} divisor function, and N,XN,X are large. Our main result is that the expected asymptotic for the first three sums holds for almost all h∈[−H,H]h\in[-H,H], provided that Xσ+ε≤H≤X1−εX^{\sigma+\varepsilon}\leq H\leq X^{1-\varepsilon} for some ε>0\varepsilon>0, where σ≔833=0.2424​…\sigma\coloneqq{\frac{8}{33}=0.2424\dots}, with an error term saving on average an arbitrary power of the logarithm over the trivial bound. This improves upon results of Mikawa, Perelli-Pintz, and Baier-Browning-Marasingha-Zhao, who obtained statements of this form with σ\sigma replaced by 13\frac{1}{3}. We obtain an analogous result for the fourth sum for most NN in an interval of the form [X,X+H][X,X+H] with Xσ+ε≤H≤X1−εX^{\sigma+\varepsilon}\leq H\leq X^{1-\varepsilon}.

Our method starts with a variant of an argument from a paper of Zhan, using the circle method and some oscillatory integral estimates to reduce matters to establishing some mean-value estimates for certain Dirichlet polynomials associated to “Type d3d_{3}” and “Type d4d_{4}” sums (as well as some other sums that are easier to treat). After applying Hölder’s inequality to the Type d3d_{3} sum, one is left with two expressions, one of which we can control using a short interval mean value theorem of Jutila, and the other we can control using exponential sum estimates of Robert and Sargos. The Type d4d_{4} sum is treated similarly using the classical L2L^{2} mean value theorem and the classical van der Corput exponential sum estimates.

In a sequel to this paper we will obtain related results for the correlations involving dk​(n)d_{k}(n) for much smaller values of HH but with weaker bounds.

1. Introduction

This paper (as well as the sequel [53]) will be concerned with the asymptotic estimation of correlations of the form

(1) ∑X<n≤2​Xf⁡(n)​g⁡(n+h)¯\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}f(n)\overline{g(n+h)}

for various functions f,g:ℤ→ℂf,g\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} and large XX, and for “most” integers hh in the range |h|≤H|h|\leq H for some H=H⁡(X)H=H(X) growing in XX at a moderate rate; in this paper we will mostly be concerned with the regime where H=XθH=X^{\theta} for some fixed 0<θ<10<\theta<1. We will focus our attention on the particularly well studied correlations

(2) ∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)\displaystyle\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n) Λ⁡(n+h)\displaystyle\Lambda(n+h)
(3) ∑X<n≤2​Xdk​(n)\displaystyle\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}d_{k}(n) dl​(n+h)\displaystyle d_{l}(n+h)
(4) ∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)\displaystyle\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n) dk​(n+h)\displaystyle d_{k}(n+h)
(5) ∑nΛ⁡(n)\displaystyle\sum_{n}\Lambda(n) Λ⁡(X−n)\displaystyle\Lambda(X-n)

for fixed k,l≥2k,l\geq 2, where Λ\Lambda is the von Mangoldt function and

dk​(n)≔∑n1​⋯​nk=n1d_{k}(n)\coloneqq\sum_{n_{1}\dotsm n_{k}=n}1

is the kthk^{\operatorname{th}} divisor function, adopting the convention that Λ⁡(n)=dk​(n)=0\Lambda(n)=d_{k}(n)=0 for n≤0n\leq 0. Of course, to interpret (5) properly one needs to take XX to be an integer, and then one can split this expression by symmetry into what is essentially twice a sum of the form (1) with XX replaced by X/2X/2, f⁡(n)≔Λ⁡(n)f(n)\coloneqq\Lambda(n), g⁡(n)≔Λ⁡(−n)g(n)\coloneqq\Lambda(-n), and h≔−Xh\coloneqq-X. One can also work with the range 1≤n≤X1\leq n\leq X rather than X<n≤2​XX<n\leq 2X for (2), (3), (4) with only minor changes to the arguments below. As is well known, the von Mangoldt function Λ\Lambda behaves similarly in many ways to the divisor functions dkd_{k} for kk moderately large, with identities such as the Linnik identity [46] and the Heath-Brown identity [28] providing an explicit connection between the two functions. Because of this, we will be able to treat both Λ\Lambda and dkd_{k} in a largely unified fashion.

In the regime when hh is fixed and non-zero, and XX goes to infinity, we have well established conjectures for the asymptotic values of each of the above expressions:

Conjecture 1.1.

Let hh be a fixed non-zero integer, and let k,l≥2k,l\geq 2 be fixed natural numbers.

  • (i)

    (Hardy-Littlewood prime tuples conjecture [24]) We have11 1 See Section 2 for the asymptotic notation used in this paper.

    (6) ∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)​Λ​(n+h)=𝔖⁡(h)​X+O⁡(X1/2+o⁡(1))\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n)\Lambda(n+h)={\mathfrak{S}}(h)X+O(X^{1/2+o(1)})

    as X→∞X\to\infty, where the singular series 𝔖⁡(h){\mathfrak{S}}(h) vanishes if hh is odd, and is equal to

    (7) 𝔖(h)≔2Π2∏p|h:p>2p−1p−2{\mathfrak{S}}(h)\coloneqq 2\Pi_{2}\prod_{p|h:p>2}\frac{p-1}{p-2}

    when hh is even, where Π2≔∏p>2(1−1(p−1)2)\Pi_{2}\coloneqq\prod_{p>2}(1-\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}) is the twin prime constant.

  • (ii)

    (Divisor correlation conjecture [77], [34], [9, Conjecture 3]) We have22 2 In [77] it is conjectured (in the k=lk=l case) that the error term is only bounded by O⁡(x1−1/k+o⁡(1))O(x^{1-1/k+o(1)}), and in [34] it is in fact conjectured that the error term is not better than this; see also [36] for further discussion. Interestingly, in the function field case (replacing ℤ\mathbb{Z} by Fq​[t]F_{q}[t]) the error term was bounded by O(q−1/2)O(q^{-1/2}) times the main term in the large qq limit in [1], but this only gives square root cancellation in the degree 11 case n=1n=1 and so does not seem to give strong guidance as to the size of the error term in the large nn limit.

    (8) ∑X<n≤2​Xdk​(n)​dl​(n+h)=Pk,l,h​(log⁡X)​X+O⁡(X1/2+o⁡(1))\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}d_{k}(n)d_{l}(n+h)=P_{k,l,h}(\log X)X+O(X^{1/2+o(1)})

    as X→∞X\to\infty, for some polynomial Pk,l,hP_{k,l,h} of degree k+l−2k+l-2.

    (9) ∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)​dk​(n+h)=Qk,h​(log⁡X)​X+O⁡(X1/2+o⁡(1))\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n)d_{k}(n+h)=Q_{k,h}(\log X)X+O(X^{1/2+o(1)})

    as X→∞X\to\infty, for some polynomial Qk,hQ_{k,h} of degree k−1k-1.

    (Quantitative Goldbach conjecture, see e.g. [38, Ch. 19]) We have

    (10) ∑nΛ⁡(n)​Λ​(X−n)=𝔖⁡(X)​X+O⁡(X1/2+o⁡(1))\sum_{n}\Lambda(n)\Lambda(X-n)={\mathfrak{S}}(X)X+O(X^{1/2+o(1)})

    as X→∞X\to\infty, where 𝔖⁡(X){\mathfrak{S}}(X) was defined in (7) and XX is restricted to be integer.

Remark 1.2.

The polynomials Pk,l,hP_{k,l,h} are in principle computable (see [9] for an explicit formula), but they become quite messy in their lower order terms. For instance, a classical result of Ingham [33] shows that the leading term in the quadratic polynomial P2,2,h​(t)P_{2,2,h}(t) is (6π2​∑d|h1d)​t2(\frac{6}{\pi^{2}}\sum_{d|h}\frac{1}{d})t^{2}, but the lower order terms of this polynomial, computed in [15] (with the sum ∑X<n≤2​X\sum_{X<n\leq 2X} replaced with the closely related sum ∑n≤X\sum_{n\leq X}), are significantly more complicated. A similar situation occurs for Qk,hQ_{k,h}; see for instance [17] for an explicit formula for Q2,hQ_{2,h}. The top degree terms of Pk,l,h,Qk,hP_{k,l,h},Q_{k,h} are however easy to predict from standard probablistic heuristics: one should have

(11) Pk,l,h​(t)=tk−1(k−1)!​tl−1(l−1)!​(∏p𝔖k,l,p​(h))+Ok,l,h​(tk+l−3)P_{k,l,h}(t)=\frac{t^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}\frac{t^{l-1}}{(l-1)!}\left(\prod_{p}{\mathfrak{S}}_{k,l,p}(h)\right)+O_{k,l,h}(t^{k+l-3})

and

Qk,h​(t)=tk−1(k−1)!​(∏p𝔖k,p​(h))+Ok,h​(tk−2)Q_{k,h}(t)=\frac{t^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}\left(\prod_{p}{\mathfrak{S}}_{k,p}(h)\right)+O_{k,h}(t^{k-2})

where the local factors 𝔖k,l,p​(h),𝔖k,p​(h){\mathfrak{S}}_{k,l,p}(h),{\mathfrak{S}}_{k,p}(h) are defined by the formulae33 3 One can simplify these formulae slightly by observing that 𝔼​dk,p​(𝐧)=(1−1p)1−k\mathbb{E}d_{k,p}({\mathbf{n}})=(1-\frac{1}{p})^{1-k} and 𝔼​Λp​(𝐧)=1\mathbb{E}\Lambda_{p}({\bf n})=1.

𝔖k,l,p​(h)≔𝔼​dk,p​(𝐧)​dl,p​(𝐧+h)𝔼​dk,p​(𝐧)​𝔼​dl,p​(𝐧){\mathfrak{S}}_{k,l,p}(h)\coloneqq\frac{\mathbb{E}d_{k,p}({\mathbf{n}})d_{l,p}({\mathbf{n}}+h)}{\mathbb{E}d_{k,p}({\mathbf{n}})\mathbb{E}d_{l,p}({\mathbf{n}})}

and

𝔖k,p​(h)≔𝔼​dk,p​(𝐧)​Λp​(𝐧+h)𝔼​dk,p​(𝐧)​𝔼​Λp​(𝐧){\mathfrak{S}}_{k,p}(h)\coloneqq\frac{\mathbb{E}d_{k,p}({\mathbf{n}})\Lambda_{p}({\mathbf{n}}+h)}{\mathbb{E}d_{k,p}({\mathbf{n}})\mathbb{E}\Lambda_{p}({\mathbf{n}})}

where 𝐧{\mathbf{n}} is a random variable drawn from the profinite integers ℤ^\hat{\mathbb{Z}} with uniform Haar probability measure, dk,p​(𝐧)≔(vp​(𝐧)+k−1k−1)d_{k,p}({\mathbf{n}})\coloneqq\binom{v_{p}({\mathbf{n}})+k-1}{k-1} is the local component of dkd_{k} at pp (with the pp-valuation vp​(𝐧)v_{p}({\mathbf{n}}) being the supremum of all jj such that pjp^{j} divides 𝐧{\mathbf{n}}), and Λp​(𝐧)≔pp−1​1p∤𝐧\Lambda_{p}({\mathbf{n}})\coloneqq\frac{p}{p-1}1_{p\nmid{\mathbf{n}}} is the local component of Λ\Lambda. See [68] for an explanation of these heuristics and a verification of the asymptotic (11), as well as an explicit formula for the local factor 𝔖k,l,p​(h){\mathfrak{S}}_{k,l,p}(h). For comparison, it is easy to see that

𝔖⁡(h)=∏p𝔼​Λp​(𝐧)​Λp​(𝐧+h)𝔼​Λp​(𝐧)​𝔼​Λp​(𝐧){\mathfrak{S}}(h)=\prod_{p}\frac{\mathbb{E}\Lambda_{p}({\mathbf{n}})\Lambda_{p}({\mathbf{n}}+h)}{\mathbb{E}\Lambda_{p}({\mathbf{n}})\mathbb{E}\Lambda_{p}({\mathbf{n}})}

for all non-zero integers hh, and similarly

𝔖⁡(X)=∏p𝔼​Λp​(𝐧)​Λp​(X−𝐧)𝔼​Λp​(𝐧)​𝔼​Λp​(𝐧){\mathfrak{S}}(X)=\prod_{p}\frac{\mathbb{E}\Lambda_{p}({\mathbf{n}})\Lambda_{p}(X-{\mathbf{n}})}{\mathbb{E}\Lambda_{p}({\mathbf{n}})\mathbb{E}\Lambda_{p}({\mathbf{n}})}

for all non-zero integers XX.

Conjecture 1.1 is considered to be quite difficult, particularly when kk and ll are large, even if one allows the error term to be larger than X1/2+o⁡(1)X^{1/2+o(1)} (but still smaller than the main term). For instance it is a notorious open problem to obtain an asymptotic for the divisor correlations in the case k=l=3k=l=3. The objective of this paper is to obtain a weaker version of Conjecture 1.1 in which one has less control on the error terms, and one is content with obtaining the asymptotics for most hh in a given range [h0−H,h0+H][h_{0}-H,h_{0}+H], rather than for all hh. This is in analogy with our recent work on Chowla and Elliott type conjectures for bounded multiplicative functions [52], although our methods here are different44 4 In particular, the arguments in [52] rely heavily on multiplicativity in small primes, which is absent in the case of the von Mangoldt function, and in the case of the divisor functions dkd_{k} would not be strong enough to give error terms of size OA​(log−A⁡x)O_{A}(\log^{-A}x) times the main term. In any event, the arguments in this paper certainly cannot work for HH slower than log⁡X\log X even if one assumes conjectures such as the Generalized Lindelöf Hypothesis, the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis or the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture, as the h=0h=0 term would dominate all of the averages considered here.. Our ranges of hh will be shorter than those in previous literature on Conjecture 1.1, although they cannot be made arbitrarily slowly growing with XX as was the case for bounded multiplicative functions in [52]. In particular, the methods in this paper will certainly be unable to unconditionally handle intervals of length X1/6−εX^{1/6-\varepsilon} or shorter for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, since it is not even known55 5 See [80] for the best known result in this direction. currently if the prime number theorem is valid in most intervals of the form [X,X+X1/6−ε][X,X+X^{1/6-\varepsilon}], and such a result would easily follow from an averaging argument (using a well-known calculation of Gallagher [21]) if we knew the prime tuples conjecture (6) for most h=O⁡(X1/6−ε)h=O(X^{1/6-\varepsilon}). However, one can do much better than this if one assumes powerful conjectures such as the Generalized Lindelöf Hypothesis (GLH), the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), or the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture (EH). We plan to discuss some of these conditional results in more detail on another occasion.

In the case of the divisor correlation conjecture (8) and the higher order Titchmarsh divisor problem (9), we can obtain much smaller values of HH (but with a much weaker error term) by a different method related to [50] and [52]. We will address this question in the sequel [53] to this paper.

1.1. Prior results

We now discuss some partial progress on each of the four parts to Conjecture 1.1, starting with the prime tuples conjecture (6). The conjecture (6) is trivial for odd hh, so we now restrict attention to even hh. In this case, even the weaker estimate

(12) ∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)​Λ​(n+h)=𝔖⁡(h)​X+o⁡(X)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n)\Lambda(n+h)={\mathfrak{S}}(h)X+o(X)

is not known to hold for any single choice of hh; for instance, the case h=2h=2 would imply the twin prime conjecture, which remains open. One can of course still use sieve theoretic methods (see e.g. [60, Corollary 3.14]) to obtain the upper bound

∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)​Λ​(n+h)≪𝔖⁡(h)​X\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n)\Lambda(n+h)\ll{\mathfrak{S}}(h)X

uniformly for |h|≤X|h|\leq X (say).

There are a number of results [10], [44], [4], [78], [57], [70], [41] that show that (6) holds for “most” hh with |h|≤H|h|\leq H, as long as HH grows moderately quickly with XX. The best known result in the literature (with respect to the range of HH) is by Mikawa [57] and Perelli-Pintz [70], who showed (in our notation) that if X1/3+ε≤H≤X1−εX^{1/3+\varepsilon}\leq H\leq X^{1-\varepsilon} for some66 6 One can also handle the range X1−ε≤H≤XX^{1-\varepsilon}\leq H\leq X by the same methods; see [57] or [70]. However, we restrict HH to be slightly smaller than XX here in order to avoid some minor technicalities arising from the fact that n+hn+h might have a slightly different magnitude than nn. This becomes relevant when dealing with the dkd_{k} functions, whose average value depends on the magnitude of the argument. fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0, then the estimate (12) holds for all but OA,ε​(H​log−A​X)O_{A,\varepsilon}(H\log^{-A}X) values of hh with |h|≤H|h|\leq H, for any fixed AA; in fact the o⁡(X)o(X) error term in (12) can also be taken to be of the form OA,ε​(X​log−A​X)O_{A,\varepsilon}(X\log^{-A}X).

Now we turn to the divisor correlation conjecture (8). These correlations have been studied by many authors [32], [33], [15], [46], [27], [62], [63], [64], [65], [42], [12], [13], [75], [19], [34], [35], [9], [36], [56], [6], [14], [68]. When k=2k=2, the conjecture is known to be true with a somewhat worse error term. For instance in the case k=l=2k=l=2 the current record is

∑X<n≤2​Xd2​(n)​d2​(n+h)\displaystyle\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}d_{2}(n)d_{2}(n+h) =P2,2,h​(log⁡X)​X+O⁡(X2/3+o⁡(1))\displaystyle=P_{2,2,h}(\log X)X+O(X^{2/3+o(1)})

as X→∞X\to\infty. This result is due to Deshouillers-Iwaniec [13]. In the cases l≥3l\geq 3, a power savings

∑X<n≤2​Xd2​(n)​dl​(n+h)=P2,l,h​(log⁡X)​X+O⁡(X1−δl+o⁡(1))\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}d_{2}(n)d_{l}(n+h)=P_{2,l,h}(\log X)X+O(X^{1-\delta_{l}+o(1)})

for exponents δl>0\delta_{l}>0, is known [6], [14], [76]. See [14], [68] for further references and surveys of the problem. Finally, we remark that a function field analogue of (8) has been established in [1], but with an error term that is only bounded by Ok,l(q−1/2)O_{k,l}(q^{-1/2}) times the main term (so the result pertains to the “large qq limit” rather than the “large nn limit”).

When k,l≥3k,l\geq 3, no unconditional proof of even the weaker asymptotic

∑X<n≤2​Xdk​(n)​dl​(n+h)=Pk,l,h​(log⁡X)​X+o⁡(X​logk+l−2​X)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}d_{k}(n)d_{l}(n+h)=P_{k,l,h}(\log X)X+o(X\log^{k+l-2}X)

is known. However, upper and lower bounds of the correct order of magnitude are available; see for example, [30, 31, 54, 55, 67, 68].

In the case k=l=3k=l=3, the analogue of Mikawa’s and Perelli-Pintz’s results (now with a power savings in error terms) were recently established by Baier, Browning, Marasingha, and Zhao [3], who were able to obtain the asymptotic

∑X<n≤2​Xd3​(n)​d3​(n+h)=P3,3,h​(log⁡X)​X+O⁡(X1−δ)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}d_{3}(n)d_{3}(n+h)=P_{3,3,h}(\log X)X+O(X^{1-\delta})

for all but Oε​(H​X−δ)O_{\varepsilon}(HX^{-\delta}) choices of hh with |h|≤H|h|\leq H, provided that X1/3+ε≤H≤X1−εX^{1/3+\varepsilon}\leq H\leq X^{1-\varepsilon} for some fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0, and δ>0\delta>0 is a small exponent depending only on ε\varepsilon.

Next, we turn to the (higher order) Titchmarsh divisor problem (9). This problem is often expressed in terms of computing an asymptotic for ∑p≤Xdk​(p+h)\sum_{p\leq X}d_{k}(p+h) rather than ∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)​dk​(n+h)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n)d_{k}(n+h), but the two sums can be related to each other via summation by parts up to negligible error terms, so it is fairly easy to translate results about one sum to the other. The k=2k=2 case of (9) with qualitative error term was established by Linnik [46]. This result was improved by Fouvry [18] and Bombieri-Friedlander-Iwaniec [5], who in our notation showed that

∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)​d2​(n+h)=Q2,h​(log⁡X)​X+OA​(X​log−A​X)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n)d_{2}(n+h)=Q_{2,h}(\log X)X+O_{A}(X\log^{-A}X)

for any A>0A>0. Recently, Drappeau [14] showed that the error term could be improved to O⁡(X​exp⁡(−c​log⁡X))O(X\exp(-c\sqrt{\log X})) for some c>0c>0 provided that one added a correction term in the case of a Siegel zero; under the assumption of GRH, the error term could be improved further to O⁡(X1−δ)O(X^{1-\delta}) for some absolute constant δ>0\delta>0. Fiorilli [17] also established some uniformity of the error term in the parameter hh. A function field analog of (9) was proven (for arbitrary kk) in [1], but with an error term that is Ok(q−1/2)O_{k}(q^{-1/2}) times the main term.

When k≥3k\geq 3 even the weaker estimate

∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)​dk​(n+h)=Qk,h​(log⁡X)​X+o⁡(X​logk−1​X)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n)d_{k}(n+h)=Q_{k,h}(\log X)X+o(X\log^{k-1}X)

remains open; sieve theoretic methods would only give this asymptotic assuming a level of distribution of Λ\Lambda that is greater than 1−1/k1-1/k, which would follow from EH but is not known unconditionally for any k≥3k\geq 3, even after the recent breakthrough of Zhang [82] (see also [7]).

In analogy with the results of Baier, Browning, Marasingha, and Zhao [3], it is likely that the method of Mikawa [57] or Perelli-Pintz [70] can be extended to give an asymptotic of the form

∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)​d3​(n+h)=Q3,h​(log⁡X)​X+OA,ε​(X​log−A​X)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n)d_{3}(n+h)=Q_{3,h}(\log X)X+O_{A,\varepsilon}(X\log^{-A}X)

for all but OA,ε​(H​log−A​X)O_{A,\varepsilon}(H\log^{-A}X) values of hh with |h|≤H|h|\leq H, for any fixed AA, if X1/3+ε≤H≤X1−εX^{1/3+\varepsilon}\leq H\leq X^{1-\varepsilon} for some fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0; however to our knowledge this result has not been explicitly proven in the literature.

Finally, we discuss some known results on the Goldbach conjecture (10). As with the prime tuples conjecture, standard sieve methods (e.g. [60, Theorem 3.13]) will give the upper bound

∑nΛ⁡(n)​Λ​(X−n)≪𝔖⁡(X)​X\sum_{n}\Lambda(n)\Lambda(X-n)\ll{\mathfrak{S}}(X)X

uniformly in XX. There are a number of results [74], [10], [16], [61], [8], [45], [47] establishing that the left-hand side of (10) is positive for “most” large even integers XX; for instance, in [47] it was shown that this was the case for all but O⁡(X00.879)O(X_{0}^{0.879}) of even integers X≤X0X\leq X_{0}, for any large X0X_{0}. There are analogous results in shorter intervals [69], [48], [79], [39], [25], [49]; for instance in [49] it was shown that for any 1/5<θ≤11/5<\theta\leq 1 the left-hand side of (10) is positive for all but O⁡(X0θ−δ)O(X_{0}^{\theta-\delta}) even integers X∈[X0,X0+X0θ]X\in[X_{0},X_{0}+X_{0}^{\theta}], for some δ>0\delta>0 depending on θ\theta, while in [25, Chapter 10] it is shown that for 11180≤θ≤1\frac{11}{180}\leq\theta\leq 1 and A>0A>0, the left-hand side of (10) is positive for all but OA​(X0​log−A​X0)O_{A}(X_{0}\log^{-A}X_{0}) even integers X∈[X0,X0+X0δ]X\in[X_{0},X_{0}+X_{0}^{\delta}]. On the other hand, if one wants the left-hand side of (10) to not just be positive, but be close to the main term 𝔖⁡(X)​X{\mathfrak{S}}(X)X on the right-hand side, the state of the art requires larger intervals. For instance, in [38, Proposition 19.5] it is shown that (10) holds (with OA​(X0​log−A​X0)O_{A}(X_{0}\log^{-A}X_{0}) error term) for all but OA​(X0​log−A​X0)O_{A}(X_{0}\log^{-A}X_{0}) even integers XX in [1,X0][1,X_{0}]. In [70], Perelli and Pintz obtained a similar result for the intervals [X0,X0+X013+ε][X_{0},X_{0}+X_{0}^{\frac{1}{3}+\varepsilon}] for any ε>0\varepsilon>0. In [26], Halupczok obtains variants of the result of Perelli-Pintz with the additional requirement that one of the prime in n=p1+p2n=p_{1}+p_{2} is constrained to a short interval or an arithmetic progression with large moduli.

1.2. New results

Our main result is as follows: for all four correlations (i)-(iv) in Conjecture 1.1, we can improve upon the results of Mikawa, Perelli-Pintz, and Baier-Browning-Marasingha-Zhao by improving the exponent 13\frac{1}{3} to the quantity

(13) σ≔833=0.2424​…;\sigma\coloneqq{\frac{8}{33}=0.2424\dots};

for future reference we observe that σ\sigma lies in the range

(14) 15<1148<730<σ<14.\frac{1}{5}<\frac{11}{48}<\frac{7}{30}<\sigma<\frac{1}{4}.

(The significance of the other fractions in (14) will become more apparent later in the paper.) More precisely, we have

Theorem 1.3 (Averaged correlations).

Let A>0A>0, 0<ε<1/20<\varepsilon<1/2 and k,l≥2k,l\geq 2 be fixed, and suppose that Xσ+ε≤H≤X1−εX^{\sigma+\varepsilon}\leq H\leq X^{1-\varepsilon} for some X≥2X\geq 2, where σ\sigma is defined by (13). Let 0≤h0≤X1−ε0\leq h_{0}\leq X^{1-\varepsilon}.

  • (i)

    (Averaged Hardy-Littlewood conjecture) One has

    ∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)​Λ​(n+h)=𝔖⁡(h)​X+OA,ε​(X​log−A​X)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n)\Lambda(n+h)={\mathfrak{S}}(h)X+O_{A,\varepsilon}(X\log^{-A}X)

    for all but OA,ε​(H​log−A​X)O_{A,\varepsilon}(H\log^{-A}X) values of hh with |h−h0|≤H|h-h_{0}|\leq H.

  • (ii)

    (Averaged divisor correlation conjecture) One has

    ∑X<n≤2​Xdk​(n)​dl​(n+h)=Pk,l,h​(log⁡X)​X+OA,ε,k,l​(X​log−A​X)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}d_{k}(n)d_{l}(n+h)=P_{k,l,h}(\log X)X+O_{A,\varepsilon,k,l}(X\log^{-A}X)

    for all but OA,ε,k,l​(H​log−A​X)O_{A,\varepsilon,k,l}(H\log^{-A}X) values of hh with |h−h0|≤H|h-h_{0}|\leq H.

  • (iii)

    (Averaged higher order Titchmarsh divisor problem) One has

    ∑X<n≤2​XΛ⁡(n)​dk​(n+h)=Qk,h​(log⁡X)​X+OA,ε,k​(X​log−A​X)\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}\Lambda(n)d_{k}(n+h)=Q_{k,h}(\log X)X+O_{A,\varepsilon,k}(X\log^{-A}X)

    for all but OA,ε,k​(H​log−A​X)O_{A,\varepsilon,k}(H\log^{-A}X) values of hh with |h−h0|≤H|h-h_{0}|\leq H.

  • (iv)

    (Averaged Goldbach conjecture) One has

    ∑nΛ⁡(n)​Λ​(N−n)=𝔖⁡(N)​N+OA,ε​(X​log−A​X)\sum_{n}\Lambda(n)\Lambda(N-n)={\mathfrak{S}}(N)N+O_{A,\varepsilon}(X\log^{-A}X)

    for all but OA,ε​(H​log−A​X)O_{A,\varepsilon}(H\log^{-A}X) integers NN in the interval [X,X+H][X,X+H].

In the case of correlations of the divisor functions, our method can be modified to obtain power-savings in the error terms. However, since we cannot obtain power-savings in the case of correlations of the von Mangoldt function, in order to keep our choice of parameters uniform accross the four cases stated in Theorem 1.3 we have decided to state the result for the divisor function with weaker error terms (see Remark 1.5 below for more details).

As mentioned previously, the cases H≥X13+εH\geq X^{\frac{1}{3}+\varepsilon} of the above theorem are essentially in the literature, either being contained in the papers of Mikawa [57] Perelli-Pintz [70] and Baier et al. [3], or following from a modification of their methods. We give a slightly different proof on these cases in this paper. Still another, but related, proof of the H≥X13+εH\geq X^{\frac{1}{3}+\varepsilon} cases could be obtained by adapting arguments used previously for studying the Goldbach problem in short intervals, see e.g. [25, Chapter 10] for such arguments. In the range H>X13+εH>X^{\frac{1}{3}+\varepsilon} our argument relies only on standard mean-value theorems and on a simple bound for the fourth moment of Dirichlet LL-functions (which follows from the mean-value theorem and Poisson summation formula). In contrast, the approaches in [57, 3, 70] depend in the range H>X1/3+εH>X^{1/3+\varepsilon} on some non-trivial input, such as either bounds for the sixth moment of the Riemann zeta-function off the half-line (in [3]), zero-density estimates (in [70]) or estimates for Kloosterman sums (in [57]). In fact our approach is entirely independent of results on Kloosterman sums, even for smaller HH (see Remark 1.4 below for more details).

Before we embark on a discussion of the proof, we note that our results do not appear to have new consequences for moments of the Riemann-zeta function. For instance for the problem of estimating the sixth moment of the Riemann zeta-function one needs an estimate for

(15) ∑h≤H∑n≤Xd3​(n)​d3​(n+h)\sum_{h\leq H}\sum_{n\leq X}d_{3}(n)d_{3}(n+h)

in the range H=X1/3H=X^{1/3}. To obtain an improvement over the best-known estimate

∫T2​T|ζ⁡(12+i​t)|6​𝑑t≪T5/4+ε\int_{T}^{2T}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^{6}dt\ll T^{5/4+\varepsilon}

one would need to show that in the range H=X1/3H=X^{1/3} the error term in (15) is ≪H​X5/6−ε\ll HX^{5/6-\varepsilon}. A naive application of our result, gives a bound of ≪AHX(logX)−A\ll_{A}HX(\log X)^{-A} for the error term. As we pointed out earlier in the case of the divisor function, it is possible to improve the (log⁡X)−A(\log X)^{-A} to X−δX^{-\delta} for some δ>0\delta>0, however since our method is optimized for dealing with smaller HH, rather than with H=X1/3H=X^{1/3} we doubt that there will be new results in this range.

We now briefly summarize the arguments used to prove Theorem 1.3. To follow the many changes of variable of summation (or integration) in the argument, it is convenient to refer to the following diagram:

Additive frequency ​αMultiplicative frequency ​t⇕⇕Position ​n⇔Logarithmic position ​u\left.\begin{array}[]{ccc}\text{Additive frequency }\alpha&&\text{Multiplicative frequency }t\\ \Updownarrow&&\Updownarrow\\ \text{Position }n&\Leftrightarrow&\text{Logarithmic position }u\end{array}\right.

Initially, the correlations studied in Theorem 1.3 are expressed in terms of the position variable nn (an integer comparable to XX), which we have placed in the bottom left of the above diagram. The first step in analyzing these correlations, which is standard, is to apply the Hardy-Littlewood circle method (i.e., the Fourier transform), which expresses correlations such as (1) as an integral

∫𝕋Sf​(α)​Sg​(α)¯​e​(α​h)​𝑑α\int_{\mathbb{T}}S_{f}(\alpha)\overline{S_{g}(\alpha)}e(\alpha h)\ d\alpha

over the unit circle 𝕋≔ℝ/ℤ\mathbb{T}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}, where Sf,SgS_{f},S_{g} are the exponential sums

Sf​(α)\displaystyle S_{f}(\alpha) ≔∑X<n≤2​Xf⁡(n)​e​(n​α)\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}f(n)e(n\alpha)
Sg​(α)\displaystyle S_{g}(\alpha) ≔∑X<n≤2​Xg⁡(n)​e​(n​α).\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{X<n\leq 2X}g(n)e(n\alpha).

The additive frequency α\alpha, which is the Fourier-analytic dual to the position variable nn, is depicted on the top left of the above diagram. In our applications, ff will be of the form Λ​1(X,2​X]\Lambda 1_{(X,2X]} or dk​1(X,2​X]d_{k}1_{(X,2X]}, and similarly for gg. We then divide 𝕋\mathbb{T} into the major arcs, in which |α−aq|≤logB′⁡XX|\alpha-\frac{a}{q}|\leq\frac{\log^{B^{\prime}}X}{X} for some q≤logB⁡Xq\leq\log^{B}X, and the minor arcs, which consist of all other α\alpha. Here B′>B>0B^{\prime}>B>0 are suitable large constants (depending on the parameters A,k,lA,k,l).

The major arcs contribute the main terms 𝔖⁡(h)​X{\mathfrak{S}}(h)X, Pk,l,h​(log⁡X)​XP_{k,l,h}(\log X)X, Qk,h​(log⁡X)​XQ_{k,h}(\log X)X, 𝔖⁡(N)​N{\mathfrak{S}}(N)N to Theorem 1.3, and the estimation of their contribution is standard; we do this in Section 4. The main novelty in our arguments lies in the treatment of the minor arc contribution, which we wish to show is negligible on the average. After an application of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the main task becomes that of estimating the integral

(16) ∫β−1/Hβ+1/H|Sf​(α)|2​𝑑α\int_{\beta-1/H}^{\beta+1/H}|S_{f}(\alpha)|^{2}\ d\alpha

for various “minor arc” β\beta. To do this, we follow a strategy from a paper of Zhan [81] and estimate this type of integral in terms of the Dirichlet series

𝒟⁡[f]​(12+i​t)≔∑nf⁡(n)n12+i​t{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it)\coloneqq\sum_{n}\frac{f(n)}{n^{\frac{1}{2}+it}}

for various “multiplicative frequencies” tt. Actually for technical reasons we will have to twist these Dirichlet series by a Dirichlet character χ\chi of small conductor, but we ignore this complication for this informal discussion. The variable tt is depicted on the top right of the above diagram, and so we will have to return to the position variable nn and then go through the logarithmic position variable uu, which we will introduce shortly.

Applying the Fourier transform (as was done by Gallagher in [20]), we can control the expression (16) in terms of an expression of the form

∫ℝ|∑x≤n≤x+Hf⁡(n)​e​(β​n)|2​𝑑x.\int_{\mathbb{R}}|\sum_{x\leq n\leq x+H}f(n)e(\beta n)|^{2}\ dx.

Actually, it is convenient to smooth the summation appearing here, but we ignore this technicality for this informal discussion. This returns one to the bottom left of the above diagram. Next, one makes the logarithmic change of variables u=log⁡n−log⁡Xu=\log n-\log X, or equivalently n=X​eun=Xe^{u}. This transforms the main variable of interest to a bounded real number u=O⁡(1)u=O(1), and the phase e⁡(β​n)e(\beta n) that appears in the above expression now takes the form e⁡(β​X​eu)e(\beta Xe^{u}). We are now at the bottom right of the diagram.

Finally, one takes the Fourier transform to convert the expression involving uu to an expression involving tt, which (up to a harmless factor of 2​π2\pi, as well as a phase modulation) is the Fourier dual of uu. Because the uu derivative of the phase β​X​eu\beta Xe^{u} is comparable in magnitude to |β|​X|\beta|X, one would expect the main contributions in the integration over tt to come from the region where tt is comparable to |β|​X|\beta|X. This intuition can be made rigorous using Fourier-analytic tools such as Littlewood-Paley projections and the method of stationary phase.

At this point, after all the harmonic analytic transformations, we come to the arithmetic heart of the problem. A precise statement of the estimates needed can be found in Proposition 5.4; a model problem is to obtain an upper bound on the quantity

∫|t|≍λ​X(∫t−λ​Ht+λ​H|𝒟⁡[f]​(12+i​t′)|​d​t′)2​𝑑t\int_{|t|\asymp\lambda X}\left(\int_{t-\lambda H}^{t+\lambda H}\left|{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it^{\prime})\right|\ dt^{\prime}\right)^{2}\ dt

for 1H≪λ≪log−B⁡X\frac{1}{H}\ll\lambda\ll\log^{-B}X that improves (by a large power of log⁡X\log X) upon the trivial bound of Ok​(λ2​H2​X​logOk​(1)​X)O_{k}(\lambda^{2}H^{2}X\log^{O_{k}(1)}X) that one can obtain from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality

(∫t−λ​Ht+λ​H|𝒟⁡[f]​(12+i​t′)|​d​t′)2≪λ​H​∫t−λ​Ht+λ​H|𝒟⁡[f]​(12+i​t′)|2​d​t′\left(\int_{t-\lambda H}^{t+\lambda H}|{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it^{\prime})|\ dt^{\prime}\right)^{2}\ll\lambda H\int_{t-\lambda H}^{t+\lambda H}|{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it^{\prime})|^{2}\ dt^{\prime}

Fubini’s theorem, and the standard L2L^{2} mean value theorem for Dirichlet polynomials. The most difficult case occurs when λ\lambda is large (e.g. λ=log−B⁡X\lambda=\log^{-B}X); indeed, the case λ≤X−16−ε\lambda\leq X^{-\frac{1}{6}-\varepsilon} of small λ\lambda is analogous to the prime number theorem in most short intervals of the form [X,X+X16+ε][X,X+X^{\frac{1}{6}+\varepsilon}], and (following [25]) can be treated by such methods as the Huxley large values estimate and mean value theorems for Dirichlet polynomials. This is done in Appendix A. (In the case f=d3​1(X,2​X]f=d_{3}1_{(X,2X]}, these bounds are essentially contained (in somewhat disguised form) in [3, Theorem 1.1].)

For sake of argument let us focus now on the case f=Λ​1(X,2​X]f=\Lambda 1_{(X,2X]}. We proceed via the usual technique of decomposing Λ\Lambda using the Heath-Brown identity [28] and further dyadic decompositions. Because σ\sigma lies in the range (14), this leaves us with “Type II” sums where ff is replaced by a Dirichlet convolution α∗β\alpha\ast\beta with α\alpha supported on [Xε2,X−ε2​H][X^{\varepsilon^{2}},X^{-\varepsilon^{2}}H], as well as “Type d1d_{1}”, “Type d2d_{2}”, “Type d3d_{3}”, and “Type d4d_{4}” sums where (roughly speaking) ff is replaced by a Dirichlet convolution that resembles one of the first four divisor functions d1,d2,d3,d4d_{1},d_{2},d_{3},d_{4} respectively. (See Proposition 6.1 for a precise statement of the estimates needed.)

The contribution of the Type II sums can be easily handled by an application of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and L2L^{2} mean value theorems for Dirichlet polynomials. The Type d1d_{1} and Type d2d_{2} sums can be treated by L4L^{4} moment theorems [71], [2] for the Riemann zeta function and Dirichlet LL-functions. These arguments are already enough to recover the results in [57], [70], [3], which treated the case H≥X1/3+εH\geq X^{1/3+\varepsilon}; our methods are slightly different from those in [57], [70], [3] due to our heavier reliance on Dirichlet polynomials. To break the X1/3X^{1/3} barrier we need to control Type d3d_{3} sums, and to go below X1/4X^{1/4} one must also consider Type d4d_{4} sums. The standard unconditional moment estimates on the Riemann zeta function and Dirichlet LL-functions are inadequate for treating the d3d_{3} sums. Instead, after applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and subdividing the range {t:t≍λ​X}\{t:t\asymp\lambda X\} into intervals of length λ​X\sqrt{\lambda X}, the problem reduces to obtaining two bounds on Dirichlet polynomials in “typical” short or medium intervals. A model for these problems would be to establish the bounds

(17) ∫tj−λ​Xtj+λ​X|𝒟[1(X1/3,2​X1/3]](12+it)|4dt≪εXε2λ​X\int_{t_{j}-\sqrt{\lambda X}}^{t_{j}+\sqrt{\lambda X}}\left|{\mathcal{D}}[1_{(X^{1/3},2X^{1/3}]}]\left(\frac{1}{2}+it\right)\right|^{4}\ dt\ll_{\varepsilon}X^{\varepsilon^{2}}\sqrt{\lambda X}

and

(18) ∫tj−Htj+H|𝒟[1(X1/3,2​X1/3]](12+it)|2dt≪εXε2H\int_{t_{j}-H}^{t_{j}+H}\left|{\mathcal{D}}[1_{(X^{1/3},2X^{1/3}]}]\left(\frac{1}{2}+it\right)\right|^{2}\ dt\ll_{\varepsilon}X^{\varepsilon^{2}}H

for “typical” j=1,…,rj=1,\dotsc,r, where t1,…,trt_{1},\dotsc,t_{r} is a maximal λ​X\sqrt{\lambda X}-separated subset of [λ​X,2​λ​X][\lambda X,2\lambda X]. (These are oversimplifications; see Proposition 7.4 and Proposition 7.5 for more precise statements of the bounds needed.)

The first estimate (17) turns out to follow readily from a fourth moment estimate of Jutila [40] for Dirichlet LL-functions in medium-sized intervals on average. As for (18), one can use the Fourier transform to bound the left-hand side by something that is roughly of the form

(19) HX1/3​∑ℓ=O⁡(X1/3/H)|∑m≍X1/3e⁡(tj2​π​log⁡m+ℓm−ℓ)|.\frac{H}{X^{1/3}}\sum_{\ell=O(X^{1/3}/H)}\left|\sum_{m\asymp X^{1/3}}e\left(\frac{t_{j}}{2\pi}\log\frac{m+\ell}{m-\ell}\right)\right|.

The diagonal term ℓ=0\ell=0 is easy to treat, so we focus on the non-zero values of ℓ\ell. By Taylor expansion, the phase tj2​π​log⁡m+ℓm−ℓ\frac{t_{j}}{2\pi}\log\frac{m+\ell}{m-\ell} is approximately equal to the monomial tjπ​ℓm\frac{t_{j}}{\pi}\frac{\ell}{m}. If one were to actually replace e⁡(tj2​π​log⁡m+ℓm−ℓ)e(\frac{t_{j}}{2\pi}\log\frac{m+\ell}{m-\ell}) by e⁡(tjπ​ℓm)e(\frac{t_{j}}{\pi}\frac{\ell}{m}), then it turns out that one can obtain a very favorable estimate by using the fourth moment bounds of Robert and Sargos [73] for exponential sums with monomial phases. Unfortunately, the Taylor expansion does contain an additional lower order term of tj3​π​ℓ3m3\frac{t_{j}}{3\pi}\frac{\ell^{3}}{m^{3}} which complicates the analysis, but it turns out that (at the cost of some inefficiency) one can still apply the bounds of Robert and Sargos to obtain a satisfactory estimate for the indicated value (13) of σ\sigma.

In the range (14) one must also treat the Type d4d_{4} sums. Here we use a cruder version of the Type d3d_{3} analysis. The analogue of Jutila’s estimate (which would now require control of sixth moments) is not known unconditionally, so we use the classical L2L^{2} mean value theorem in its place. The estimates of Robert and Sargos are now unfavorable, so we instead estimate the analogue of (19) using the classical van der Corput exponent pair (1/14,2/7)(1/14,2/7), which turns out to work even for σ\sigma as small as 7/307/30 (see (14)). Hence d4d_{4} sums turn out to be easier than d3d_{3} in our range of HH. However we are not able to estimate d4d_{4} sums in the full range X1/5+ε<H<X1/4−εX^{1/5+\varepsilon}<H<X^{1/4-\varepsilon}. Therefore there is no advantage in considering d5d_{5} sums which would appear if we wanted to take HH below X1/5−εX^{1/5-\varepsilon} (we note that we can cover a tiny region of the d5d_{5} sums by proceeding in the same manner as we do with d4d_{4} sums).

Remark 1.4.

It is interesting to note that our work does not depend at all on estimates for Kloosterman sums. While the work of Mikawa for H>X1/3+εH>X^{1/3+\varepsilon} depends on the Weil bound for Kloosterman sums, our result in the same range only uses a bound for the fourth moment of Dirichlet LL-functions The latter follows from the approximate functional equation and a mean-value theorem. In the smaller ranges of HH we use in addition estimates for short moments of Dirichlet LL-functions (due to Jutila, see Proposition 2.13 below and also Corollary 2.14) that are of the same strength as those that one obtains from using Kloosterman sums (due to Iwaniec, see [37]) and yet whose proof is independent of input from algebraic geometry or spectral theory. On the other hand we note that the arguments of Perelli-Pintz [70] for H>X1/3+εH>X^{1/3+\varepsilon} do not depend on Kloosterman sums but instead of zero-density estimates.

Remark 1.5.

As usual, the results involving Λ\Lambda will have the implied constant depend in an ineffective fashion on the parameter AA, due to our reliance on Siegel’s theorem. It may be possible to eliminate this ineffectivity (possibly after excluding some “bad” scales X≍X0X\asymp X_{0}) by introducing a separate argument (in the spirit of [29]) to handle the case of a Siegel zero, but we do not pursue this matter here. In the proof of Theorem 1.3(ii), we do not need to invoke Siegel’s theorem, and it is likely that (as in [3]) we can improve the logarithmic savings log−A⁡X\log^{-A}X to a power savings X−c​εk+lX^{-\frac{c\varepsilon}{k+l}} for some absolute constant c>0c>0 (and with effective constants) by a refinement of the argument. However, we do not do this here in order to be able to treat all four estimates in a unified fashion.

2. Notation and preliminaries

All sums and products will be over integers unless otherwise specified, with the exception of sums and products over the variable pp (or p1p_{1}, p2p_{2}, p′p^{\prime}, etc.) which will be over primes. To accommodate this convention, we adopt the further convention that all functions on the natural numbers are automatically extended by zero to the rest of the integers, e.g. Λ⁡(n)=0\Lambda(n)=0 for n≤0n\leq 0.

We use A=O⁡(B)A=O(B), A≪BA\ll B, or B≫AB\gg A to denote the bound |A|≤C​B|A|\leq CB for some constant CC. If we permit CC to depend on additional parameters then we will indicate this by subscripts, thus for instance A=Ok,ε​(B)A=O_{k,\varepsilon}(B) or A≪k,εBA\ll_{k,\varepsilon}B denotes the bound |A|≤Ck,ε​B|A|\leq C_{k,\varepsilon}B for some Ck,εC_{k,\varepsilon} depending on k,εk,\varepsilon. If A,BA,B both depend on some large parameter XX, we say that A=o⁡(B)A=o(B) as X→∞X\to\infty if one has |A|≤c⁡(X)​B|A|\leq c(X)B for some function c⁡(X)c(X) of XX (as well as further “fixed” parameters not depending on XX), which goes to zero as X→∞X\to\infty (holding all “fixed” parameters constant). We also write A≍BA\asymp B for A≪B≪AA\ll B\ll A, with the same subscripting conventions as before.

We use 𝕋≔ℝ/ℤ\mathbb{T}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} to denote the unit circle, and e:𝕋→ℂe:\mathbb{T}\to\mathbb{C} to denote the fundamental character

e⁡(x)≔e2​π​i​x.e(x)\coloneqq e^{2\pi ix}.

We use 1E1_{E} to denote the indicator of a set EE, thus 1E​(n)=11_{E}(n)=1 when n∈En\in E and 1E​(n)=01_{E}(n)=0 otherwise. Similarly, if SS is a statement, we let 1S1_{S} denote the number 11 when SS is true and 00 when SS is false, thus for instance 1E​(n)=1n∈E1_{E}(n)=1_{n\in E}. If EE is a finite set, we use #​E\#E to denote its cardinality.

We use (a,b)(a,b) and [a,b][a,b] for the greatest common divisor and least common multiple of natural numbers a,ba,b respectively, and write a|ba|b if aa divides bb. We also write a=b⁡(q)a=b\ (q) if aa and bb have the same residue modulo qq.

Given a sequence f:X→ℂf:X\to\mathbb{C} on a set XX, we define the ℓp\ell^{p} norm ‖f‖ℓp\|f\|_{\ell^{p}} of ff for any 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty as

‖f‖ℓp≔(∑n∈X|f⁡(n)|p)1/p\|f\|_{\ell^{p}}\coloneqq\left(\sum_{n\in X}|f(n)|^{p}\right)^{1/p}

and similarly define the ℓ∞\ell^{\infty} norm

‖f‖ℓ∞≔supn∈X|f⁡(n)|.\|f\|_{\ell^{\infty}}\coloneqq\sup_{n\in X}|f(n)|.

Given two arithmetic functions f,g:ℕ→ℂf,g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C}, the Dirichlet convolution f∗gf\ast g is defined by

f∗g⁡(n)≔∑d|nf⁡(d)​g​(nd).f\ast g(n)\coloneqq\sum_{d|n}f(d)g\left(\frac{n}{d}\right).

2.1. Summation by parts and exponential sums

If one has an asymptotic of the form ∑X≤n≤X′′g⁡(n)≈∫XX′′h⁡(x)​𝑑x\sum_{X\leq n\leq X^{\prime\prime}}g(n)\approx\int_{X}^{X^{\prime\prime}}h(x)\ dx for all X≤X′′≤X′X\leq X^{\prime\prime}\leq X^{\prime}, then one can use summation by parts to then obtain approximations of the form ∑X≤n≤X′f⁡(n)​g​(n)≈∫XX′f⁡(x)​h​(x)​𝑑x\sum_{X\leq n\leq X^{\prime}}f(n)g(n)\approx\int_{X}^{X^{\prime}}f(x)h(x)\ dx for sufficiently “slowly varying” amplitude functions f:[X,X′]→ℂf:[X,X^{\prime}]\to\mathbb{C}. The following lemma formalizes this intuition:

Lemma 2.1 (Summation by parts).

Let X≤X′X\leq X^{\prime}, and let f:[X,X′]→ℂf:[X,X^{\prime}]\to\mathbb{C} be a smooth function. Then for any function g:ℕ→ℂg:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C} and absolutely integrable h:[X,X′]→ℂh:[X,X^{\prime}]\to\mathbb{C}, we have

∑X≤n≤X′f⁡(n)​g​(n)−∫XX′f⁡(x)​h​(x)​𝑑x≤|f⁡(X′)|​E​(X′)+∫XX′|f′​(X′′)|​E​(X′′)​d​X′′\sum_{X\leq n\leq X^{\prime}}f(n)g(n)-\int_{X}^{X^{\prime}}f(x)h(x)\ dx\leq|f(X^{\prime})|E(X^{\prime})+\int_{X}^{X^{\prime}}|f^{\prime}(X^{\prime\prime})|E(X^{\prime\prime})\ dX^{\prime\prime}

where f′f^{\prime} is the derivative of ff and E⁡(X′′)E(X^{\prime\prime}) is the quantity

E⁡(X′′)≔|∑X≤n≤X′′g⁡(n)−∫XX′′h⁡(x)​𝑑x|.E(X^{\prime\prime})\coloneqq\left|\sum_{X\leq n\leq X^{\prime\prime}}g(n)-\int_{X}^{X^{\prime\prime}}h(x)\ dx\right|.
Proof.

From the fundamental theorem of calculus we have

(20) ∑X≤n≤X′f⁡(n)​g​(n)=f⁡(X′)​∑X≤n≤X′g⁡(n)−∫XX′(∑X≤n≤X′′g⁡(n))​f′​(X′′)​d​X′′\sum_{X\leq n\leq X^{\prime}}f(n)g(n)=f(X^{\prime})\sum_{X\leq n\leq X^{\prime}}g(n)-\int_{X}^{X^{\prime}}\left(\sum_{X\leq n\leq X^{\prime\prime}}g(n)\right)f^{\prime}(X^{\prime\prime})\ dX^{\prime\prime}

and similarly

∫XX′f⁡(x)​h​(x)​𝑑x=f⁡(X′)​∫XX′h⁡(x)​𝑑x−∫XX′(∫XX′′h⁡(x)​𝑑x)​f′​(X′′)​d​X′′.\int_{X}^{X^{\prime}}f(x)h(x)\ dx=f(X^{\prime})\int_{X}^{X^{\prime}}h(x)\ dx-\int_{X}^{X^{\prime}}\left(\int_{X}^{X^{\prime\prime}}h(x)\ dx\right)f^{\prime}(X^{\prime\prime})\ dX^{\prime\prime}.

Subtracting the two identities and applying the triangle inequality and Minkowski’s integral inequality, we obtain the claim. ∎

The following variant of Lemma 2.1 will also be useful. Following Robert and Sargos [73], define the maximal sum |∑X≤n≤X′g⁡(n)|∗|\sum_{X\leq n\leq X^{\prime}}g(n)|^{*} to be the expression

(21) |∑X≤n≤X′g⁡(n)|∗≔supX≤X1≤X2≤X′|∑X1≤n≤X2g⁡(n)|.\left|\sum_{X\leq n\leq X^{\prime}}g(n)\right|^{*}\coloneqq\sup_{X\leq X_{1}\leq X_{2}\leq X^{\prime}}\left|\sum_{X_{1}\leq n\leq X_{2}}g(n)\right|.
Lemma 2.2 (Summation by parts, II).

Let X≤X′X\leq X^{\prime}, let f:[X,X′]→ℂf:[X,X^{\prime}]\to\mathbb{C} be smooth, and let g:ℕ→ℂg:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C} be a sequence. Then

|∑X≤n≤X′f⁡(n)​g​(n)|∗≤|∑X≤n≤X′g⁡(n)|∗​(supX≤x≤X′|f⁡(x)|+(X′−X)​supX≤x≤X′|f′​(x)|).\left|\sum_{X\leq n\leq X^{\prime}}f(n)g(n)\right|^{*}\leq\left|\sum_{X\leq n\leq X^{\prime}}g(n)\right|^{*}\left(\sup_{X\leq x\leq X^{\prime}}|f(x)|+(X^{\prime}-X)\sup_{X\leq x\leq X^{\prime}}|f^{\prime}(x)|\right).
Proof.

Our task is to show that

|∑X1≤n≤X2f⁡(n)​g​(n)|≤|∑X≤n≤X′g⁡(n)|∗​(supX≤x≤X′|f⁡(x)|+(X′−X)​supX≤x≤X′|f′​(x)|).\left|\sum_{X_{1}\leq n\leq X_{2}}f(n)g(n)\right|\leq\left|\sum_{X\leq n\leq X^{\prime}}g(n)\right|^{*}\left(\sup_{X\leq x\leq X^{\prime}}|f(x)|+(X^{\prime}-X)\sup_{X\leq x\leq X^{\prime}}|f^{\prime}(x)|\right).

for all X≤X1≤X2≤X′X\leq X_{1}\leq X_{2}\leq X^{\prime}. The claim then follows from (20) (replacing X,X′X,X^{\prime} by X1,X2X_{1},X_{2}) and the triangle inequality and Minkowski’s integral inequality. ∎

To estimate maximal exponential sums, we will use the following estimates, contained in the work of Robert and Sargos [73]:

Lemma 2.3.

Let M≥2M\geq 2 be a natural number, and let X≥2X\geq 2 be a real number.

  • (i)

    Let φ⁡(1),…,φ⁡(M)\varphi(1),\dotsc,\varphi(M) be real numbers, let a1,…,aMa_{1},\dotsc,a_{M} be complex numbers of modulus at most one, and let 2≤Y≤X2\leq Y\leq X. Then

    ∫0X(|∑m=1Mam​e​(t​φ​(m))|∗)4​𝑑t≪X​log4​XY​∫0Y(|∑m=1Me⁡(t​φ​(m))|)4​𝑑t.\int_{0}^{X}\left(\left|\sum_{m=1}^{M}a_{m}e(t\varphi(m))\right|^{*}\right)^{4}\ dt\ll\frac{X\log^{4}X}{Y}\int_{0}^{Y}\left(\left|\sum_{m=1}^{M}e(t\varphi(m))\right|\right)^{4}\ dt.
  • (ii)

    Let θ≠0,1\theta\neq 0,1 be a real number, let ε>0\varepsilon>0, and let aM,…,a2​Ma_{M},\dotsc,a_{2M} be complex numbers of modulus at most one. Then

    ∫0X(|∑m=M2​Mame(t(mM)θ)|∗)4dt≪θ,ε(X+M)ε(M4+M2X).\int_{0}^{X}\left(\left|\sum_{m=M}^{2M}a_{m}e\left(t\left(\frac{m}{M}\right)^{\theta}\right)\right|^{*}\right)^{4}\ dt\ll_{\theta,\varepsilon}(X+M)^{\varepsilon}(M^{4}+M^{2}X).
  • (iii)

    Suppose that M≪X≪M2M\ll X\ll M^{2}. Let φ:ℝ→ℝ\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be a smooth function obeying the derivative estimates |φ(j)​(x)|≍X/Mj|\varphi^{(j)}(x)|\asymp X/M^{j} for j=1,2,3,4j=1,2,3,4 and x≍Mx\asymp M. Then

    |∑m=M2​Me⁡(φ⁡(m))|∗≪MX1/2​|∑ϵ​ℓ≍Le⁡(φ∗​(ℓ))|∗+M1/2\left|\sum_{m=M}^{2M}e(\varphi(m))\right|^{*}\ll\frac{M}{X^{1/2}}\left|\sum_{\epsilon\ell\asymp L}e(\varphi^{*}(\ell))\right|^{*}+M^{1/2}

    for some L≍XML\asymp\frac{X}{M}, where φ∗​(t)≔φ⁡(u⁡(t))−t​u​(t)\varphi^{*}(t)\coloneqq\varphi(u(t))-tu(t) is the (negative) Legendre transform of φ\varphi, uu is the inverse of the function φ′\varphi^{\prime}, and ϵ=±1\epsilon=\pm 1 denotes the sign of φ′​(x)\varphi^{\prime}(x) in the range x≍Mx\asymp M.

Proof.

Part (i) follows from the p=2p=2 case of [73, Lemma 3]. Part (ii) follows from [73, Lemma 7] when X≤M2X\leq M^{2}, and the remaining case X>M2X>M^{2} then follows from part (i). Finally, part (iii) follows from applying the van der Corput BB-process (and Lemma 2.2), see e.g. [22, Lemma 3.6] or [38, Theorem 8.16], replacing φ\varphi with −φ-\varphi if necessary to normalize the second derivative φ′′\varphi^{\prime\prime} to be positive. ∎

2.2. Divisor-bounded arithmetic functions

Let us call an arithmetic function α:ℕ→ℂ\alpha:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C} kk-divisor-bounded for some k≥0k\geq 0 if one has the pointwise bound

α(n)≪kd2k(n)logk(2+n)\alpha(n)\ll_{k}d_{2}^{k}(n)\log^{k}(2+n)

for all nn. From the elementary mean value estimate

(22) ∑1≤n≤xdl(n)k≪k,lxloglk−1(2+x),\sum_{1\leq n\leq x}d_{l}(n)^{k}\ll_{k,l}x\log^{l^{k}-1}(2+x),

valid for any k≥0k\geq 0, l≥2l\geq 2, and x≥1x\geq 1 (see e.g., [38, formula (1.80)]), we see that a kk-divisor-bounded function obeys the ℓ2\ell^{2} bounds

(23) ∑n≤xα(n)2≪kxlogOk​(1)(2+x)\sum_{n\leq x}\alpha(n)^{2}\ll_{k}x\log^{O_{k}(1)}(2+x)

for any x≥1x\geq 1. Applying (23) with α\alpha replaced by a large power of α\alpha, we conclude in particular the ℓ∞\ell^{\infty} bound

(24) supn≤xα(n)≪k,εxε\sup_{n\leq x}\alpha(n)\ll_{k,\varepsilon}x^{\varepsilon}

for any ε>0\varepsilon>0.

2.3. Dirichlet polynomials

Given any function f:ℕ→ℂf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C} supported on a finite set, we may form the Dirichlet polynomial

(25) 𝒟​[f]​(s)≔∑nf⁡(n)ns{\mathcal{D}}[f](s)\coloneqq\sum_{n}\frac{f(n)}{n^{s}}

for any complex ss; if ff has infinite support but is bounded, we can still define 𝒟⁡[f]{\mathcal{D}}[f] in the region Re​s>1\mathrm{Re}s>1. We will use a normalization in which we mostly evaluate Dirichlet polynomials on the critical line {12+i​t:t∈ℝ}\{\frac{1}{2}+it:t\in\mathbb{R}\}, but one could easily run the argument using other normalizations, for instance by evaluating all Dirichlet polynomials on the line {1+i​t:t∈ℝ}\{1+it:t\in\mathbb{R}\} instead.

We have the following standard estimate:

Lemma 2.4 (Truncated Perron formula).

Let f:ℕ→ℂf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C}, let T,X≥2T,X\geq 2, and let 1≤x≤X1\leq x\leq X.

  • (i)

    If ff is kk-divisor-bounded for some k≥0k\geq 0, and T≤X1−εT\leq X^{1-\varepsilon}, then for any 0≤σ<1−2​ε0\leq\sigma<1-2\varepsilon, one has

    ∑n≤xf⁡(n)nσ−12​π​∫−TT𝒟⁡[f]​(1+1log⁡X+i​t)​x1−σ+1log⁡X+i​t1−σ+1log⁡X+i​t​𝑑t+Ok,σ,ε​(X1−σ​logOk​(1)⁡(T​X)T).\sum_{n\leq x}\frac{f(n)}{n^{\sigma}}-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-T}^{T}{\mathcal{D}}[f](1+\frac{1}{\log X}+it)\frac{x^{1-\sigma+\frac{1}{\log X}+it}}{1-\sigma+\frac{1}{\log X}+it}\ dt+O_{k,\sigma,\varepsilon}\left(\frac{X^{1-\sigma}\log^{O_{k}(1)}(TX)}{T}\right).
  • (ii)

    If f:ℕ→ℂf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C} is supported on [X/C,C​X][X/C,CX] for some C>1C>1, then

    (26) ∑n≤xf⁡(n)=12​π​∫−TT𝒟⁡[f]​(12+i​t)​x12+i​t12+i​t​𝑑t+OC​(∑n|f⁡(n)|​min⁡(1,XT​|x−n|)).\sum_{n\leq x}f(n)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-T}^{T}{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it)\frac{x^{\frac{1}{2}+it}}{\frac{1}{2}+it}\ dt+O_{C}\left(\sum_{n}|f(n)|\min\left(1,\frac{X}{T|x-n|}\right)\right).

    In particular, if we estimate f⁡(n)f(n) pointwise by ‖f‖ℓ∞\|f\|_{\ell^{\infty}}, we have

    (27) ∑n≤xf⁡(n)=12​π​∫−TT𝒟⁡[f]​(12+i​t)​x12+i​t12+i​t​𝑑t+OC​(‖f‖ℓ∞​X​log⁡(2+T)T).\sum_{n\leq x}f(n)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-T}^{T}{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it)\frac{x^{\frac{1}{2}+it}}{\frac{1}{2}+it}\ dt+O_{C}\left(\|f\|_{\ell^{\infty}}\frac{X\log(2+T)}{T}\right).
Proof.

For (i), apply [60, Corollary 5.3] with an≔f⁡(n)nσa_{n}\coloneqq\frac{f(n)}{n^{\sigma}} and σ0≔1−σ+1log⁡X\sigma_{0}\coloneqq 1-\sigma+\frac{1}{\log X}, as well as (22). For (ii), apply [60, Corollary 5.3] instead with an≔f⁡(n)a_{n}\coloneqq f(n) and σ0≔12\sigma_{0}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}. ∎

As one technical consequence of this lemma, we can estimate the effect of truncating an arithmetic function ff on its Dirichlet series:

Corollary 2.5 (Truncating a Dirichlet series).

Suppose that f:ℕ→ℂf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C} is supported on [X/C,C​X][X/C,CX] for some X≥1X\geq 1 and C>1C>1. Let T≥1T\geq 1. Then for any interval [X1,X2][X_{1},X_{2}] and any t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, we have the pointwise bound

𝒟⁡[f​1[X1,X2]]​(12+i​t)≪∫−TTC⁡|𝒟⁡[f]​(12+i​t+i​u)|​d​u1+|u|+‖f‖ℓ∞​X1/2​log⁡(2+T)T.{\mathcal{D}}[f1_{[X_{1},X_{2}]}](\frac{1}{2}+it)\ll_{C}\int_{-T}^{T}|{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it+iu)|\frac{du}{1+|u|}+\|f\|_{\ell^{\infty}}\frac{X^{1/2}\log(2+T)}{T}.

Because the weight 11+|u|\frac{1}{1+|u|} integrates to O⁡(log⁡(2+T))O(\log(2+T)) on [−T,T][-T,T], this corollary is morally asserting that the Dirichlet polynomial of f​1[X1,X2]f1_{[X_{1},X_{2}]} is controlled by that of ff up to logarithmic factors. As such factors will be harmless in our applications, this corollary effectively allows one to dispose of truncations such as 1[X1,X2]1_{[X_{1},X_{2}]} appearing in a Dirichlet polynomial whenever desired.

Proof.

Applying Lemma 2.4(ii) with ff replaced by n↦f⁡(n)/ni​tn\mapsto f(n)/n^{it}, we have for any xx that

∑n≤xf⁡(n)ni​t=12​π​∫−TT𝒟⁡[f]​(12+i​t+i​u)​x12+i​u12+i​u​𝑑u+OC​(‖f‖ℓ∞​X​log⁡(2+T)T)\sum_{n\leq x}\frac{f(n)}{n^{it}}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-T}^{T}{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it+iu)\frac{x^{\frac{1}{2}+iu}}{\frac{1}{2}+iu}\ du+O_{C}\left(\|f\|_{\ell^{\infty}}\frac{X\log(2+T)}{T}\right)

and hence by the triangle inequality

∑n≤xf⁡(n)ni​t≪Cx1/2∫−TT|𝒟[f](12+it+iu)|d​u1+|u|+∥f∥ℓ∞X​log⁡(2+T)T.\sum_{n\leq x}\frac{f(n)}{n^{it}}\ll_{C}x^{1/2}\int_{-T}^{T}|{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it+iu)|\frac{du}{1+|u|}+\|f\|_{\ell^{\infty}}\frac{X\log(2+T)}{T}.

The claim now follows from Lemma 2.1 (with h=0h=0, g⁡(n)g(n) replaced by f⁡(n)/ni​tf(n)/n^{it}, and f⁡(x)f(x) replaced by x−1/2x^{-1/2}). ∎

2.4. Arithmetic functions with good cancellation

Let α:ℕ→ℂ\alpha\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C} be a kk-divisor-bounded function. From (23) and Cauchy-Schwarz, we see that

(28) ∑n≤x:n=a⁡(q)α⁡(n)n12+i​t≪kx1/2logOk​(1)x\sum_{n\leq x:n=a\ (q)}\frac{\alpha(n)}{n^{\frac{1}{2}+it}}\ll_{k}x^{1/2}\log^{O_{k}(1)}x

for any t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, q≥1q\geq 1, and a∈ℤa\in\mathbb{Z}. We will say that a kk-divisor-bounded function α\alpha has good cancellation if one has the improved bound

(29) ∑n≤x:n=a⁡(q)α⁡(n)n12+i​t≪k,A,B,B′x1/2log−Ax\sum_{n\leq x:n=a\ (q)}\frac{\alpha(n)}{n^{\frac{1}{2}+it}}\ll_{k,A,B,B^{\prime}}x^{1/2}\log^{-A}x

for any A,B,B′>0A,B,B^{\prime}>0, x≥2x\geq 2, q≤logB⁡xq\leq\log^{B}x, a∈ℤa\in\mathbb{Z}, and t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} with logB′⁡x≤|t|≤xB′\log^{B^{\prime}}x\leq|t|\leq x^{B^{\prime}}, provided that B′B^{\prime} is sufficiently large depending on A,B,kA,B,k.

It is clear that if α\alpha is a kk-divisor-bounded function with good cancellation, then so is its restriction α​1[X1,X2]\alpha 1_{[X_{1},X_{2}]} to any interval [X1,X2][X_{1},X_{2}]. The property of being kk-divisor-bounded with good cancellation is also basically preserved under Dirichlet convolution:

Lemma 2.6.

Let α,β\alpha,\beta be kk-divisor-bounded functions. Then α∗β\alpha\ast\beta is a (2​k+1)(2k+1)-divisor-bounded function. Furthemore, if α\alpha and β\beta both have good cancellation, then so does α∗β\alpha\ast\beta.

If, in addition, there is an NN for which α\alpha is supported on [N2,+∞][N^{2},+\infty] and β\beta is supported on [1,N][1,N], then one can omit the hypothesis that β\beta has good cancellation in the previous claim.

Proof.

Using the elementary inequality d2k1∗d2k2≤d2k1+k2+1d_{2}^{k_{1}}\ast d_{2}^{k_{2}}\leq d_{2}^{k_{1}+k_{2}+1}, we see α∗β\alpha\ast\beta is 2​k+12k+1-divisor-bounded. Next, suppose that α\alpha and β\beta have good cancellation, and let A,B,B′>0A,B,B^{\prime}>0, x≥2x\geq 2, q≤logB⁡Xq\leq\log^{B}X, a∈ℤa\in\mathbb{Z}, and t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} with logB′⁡x≤|t|≤xB′\log^{B^{\prime}}x\leq|t|\leq x^{B^{\prime}}, with B′B^{\prime} is sufficiently large depending on A,B,kA,B,k. To show that α∗β\alpha\ast\beta has good cancellation, it suffices by dyadic decomposition to show that

(30) ∑x<n≤2​x:n=a⁡(q)α∗β⁡(n)n12+i​t≪k,A,B,B′x1/2log−Ax.\sum_{x<n\leq 2x:n=a\ (q)}\frac{\alpha\ast\beta(n)}{n^{\frac{1}{2}+it}}\ll_{k,A,B,B^{\prime}}x^{1/2}\log^{-A}x.

By decomposing α\alpha into α​1[1,x]\alpha 1_{[1,\sqrt{x}]} and α​1(x,+∞)\alpha 1_{(\sqrt{x},+\infty)}, and similarly for β\beta, we may assume from the triangle inequality that at least one of α,β\alpha,\beta is supported on (x,+∞)(\sqrt{x},+\infty); by symmetry we may assume that α\alpha is so supported. The left-hand side of (30) may thus be written as

∑a=b​c​(q)∑m≪x:m=c⁡(q)β⁡(m)m12+i​t∑x/m<n≤2​x/m:n=b⁡(q)α⁡(n)n12+i​t.\sum_{a=bc\ (q)}\sum_{m\ll\sqrt{x}:m=c\ (q)}\frac{\beta(m)}{m^{\frac{1}{2}+it}}\sum_{x/m<n\leq 2x/m:n=b\ (q)}\frac{\alpha(n)}{n^{\frac{1}{2}+it}}.

Let A′>0A^{\prime}>0 be a quantity depending on A,B,kA,B,k to be chosen later. As α\alpha has good cancellation, we may bound this (for B′B^{\prime} sufficiently large depending on k,A′,Bk,A^{\prime},B) using the triangle inequality by

≪k,A′,B,B′∑a=b​c​(q)∑m≪x:m=c⁡(q)|β⁡(m)|m12(x/m)1/2log−A′(x/m);\ll_{k,A^{\prime},B,B^{\prime}}\sum_{a=bc\ (q)}\sum_{m\ll\sqrt{x}:m=c\ (q)}\frac{|\beta(m)|}{m^{\frac{1}{2}}}(x/m)^{1/2}\log^{-A^{\prime}}(x/m);

as β\beta is kk-divisor-bounded and q≤logB⁡xq\leq\log^{B}x, we may apply (22) and bound this by

≪k,A′,B,B′x12log−A′+B+Ok​(1)x.\ll_{k,A^{\prime},B,B^{\prime}}x^{\frac{1}{2}}\log^{-A^{\prime}+B+O_{k}(1)}x.

Choosing A′A^{\prime} sufficiently large depending on A,B,kA,B,k, we obtain (30). The final claim of the lemma is proven similarly, noting that the left-hand side of (30) vanishes unless x≫N2x\gg N^{2}, and hence from the support of β\beta we may already restrict α\alpha to the region (c​x,+∞)(c\sqrt{x},+\infty) for some absolute constant c>0c>0 without invoking symmetry. ∎

We have three basic examples of functions with good cancellation:

Lemma 2.7.

The constant function 11, the logarithm function L:n↦log⁡nL:n\mapsto\log n and the Möbius function μ\mu are 11-divisor-bounded with good cancellation.

From this lemma and Lemma 2.6, we also see that Λ\Lambda and dkd_{k} have good cancellation for any fixed kk.

Proof.

For the functions 1,L1,L this follows from standard van der Corput exponential sum estimates for |∑n≤xe⁡(−t2​π​log⁡(q​n+a))|∗|\sum_{n\leq x}e(-\frac{t}{2\pi}\log(qn+a))|^{*} (e.g. [38, Lemma 8.10]) and Lemma 2.2, normalizing aa to be in the range 0≤a<q0\leq a<q. Now we consider the function μ\mu. By using multiplicativity (and increasing AA as necessary) we may assume that aa is coprime to qq. By decomposition into Dirichlet characters (and again increasing AA as necessary) it suffices to show that

(31) ∑n≤xμ⁡(n)​χ​(n)n12+i​t≪k,A,B,B′x1/2log−Ax\sum_{n\leq x}\frac{\mu(n)\chi(n)}{n^{\frac{1}{2}+it}}\ll_{k,A,B,B^{\prime}}x^{1/2}\log^{-A}x

for any Dirichlet character χ\chi of period qq.

This estimate is certainly known to the experts, but as we did not find it in this form in the literature, we prove it here. The Vinogradov-Korobov zero-free region [59, §9.5] implies that L⁡(s,χ)L(s,\chi) has no zeroes in the region

{σ+it′:0<|t′|≪|t|+x2;σ≥1−cB,B′log2/3⁡|x|​(log⁡log⁡|x|)1/3}\left\{\sigma+it^{\prime}:0<|t^{\prime}|\ll|t|+x^{2};\sigma\geq 1-\frac{c_{B,B^{\prime}}}{\log^{2/3}|x|(\log\log|x|)^{1/3}}\right\}

for some cB,B′>0c_{B,B^{\prime}}>0 depending only on B,B′B,B^{\prime}. Applying the estimates in [11, §16], and shrinking cB,B′c_{B,B^{\prime}} if necessary, we obtain the crude upper bounds

L′​(s,χ)L⁡(s,χ)≪B,B′log2|x|\frac{L^{\prime}(s,\chi)}{L(s,\chi)}\ll_{B,B^{\prime}}\log^{2}|x|

in this region. Applying Perron’s formula as in [51, Lemma 2] (see also [25, Lemma 1.5]), one then has the bound

∑n≤yΛ(n)χ(n)n−i​t≪A′,B,B′ylog−A′x\sum_{n\leq y}\Lambda(n)\chi(n)n^{-it}\ll_{A^{\prime},B,B^{\prime}}y\log^{-A^{\prime}}x

for any A′>0A^{\prime}>0 and any yy with exp⁡(log3/4⁡x)≤y≤x2\exp(\log^{3/4}x)\leq y\leq x^{2} (in fact one may replace 3/43/4 here by any constant larger than 2/32/3).

To pass from Λ\Lambda to μ\mu we use a variant of the arguments used to prove Lemma 2.6 (one could also work more directly, using upper bound for 1/L⁡(s,χ)1/L(s,\chi) but we could not find the exact upper bound we need from the literature). We begin with the trivial bound

(32) ∑n≤yμ⁡(n)​χ​(n)​n−i​t≪y\sum_{n\leq y}\mu(n)\chi(n)n^{-it}\ll y

for any y>0y>0. Writing μ⁡(n)​log⁡(n)​χ​(n)​n−i​t\mu(n)\log(n)\chi(n)n^{-it} as the Dirichlet convolution of Λ⁡(n)​χ​(n)​n−i​t\Lambda(n)\chi(n)n^{-it} and −μ⁡(n)​χ​(n)​ni​t-\mu(n)\chi(n)n^{it} and using the Dirichlet hyperbola method, we conclude that

∑n≤yμ(n)lognχ(n)n−i​t≪B,B′ylog3/4x\sum_{n\leq y}\mu(n)\log n\chi(n)n^{-it}\ll_{B,B^{\prime}}y\log^{3/4}x

for any y=x1+o⁡(1)y=x^{1+o(1)}, which by Lemma 2.2 implies that

∑n≤yμ(n)χ(n)n−i​t≪B,B′ylog−1/4x\sum_{n\leq y}\mu(n)\chi(n)n^{-it}\ll_{B,B^{\prime}}y\log^{-1/4}x

for y=x1+o⁡(1)y=x^{1+o(1)}. Applying the Dirichlet hyperbola method again (using the above bound to replace the trivial bound (32) for y=x1+o⁡(1)y=x^{1+o(1)}) we conclude that

∑n≤yμ(n)χ(n)n−i​t≪B,B′ylog−2/4x\sum_{n\leq y}\mu(n)\chi(n)n^{-it}\ll_{B,B^{\prime}}y\log^{-2/4}x

for y=x1+o⁡(1)y=x^{1+o(1)}. Iterating this argument O⁡(A)O(A) times, we eventually conclude that

∑n≤yμ(n)χ(n)n−i​t≪A,B,B′ylog−Ax\sum_{n\leq y}\mu(n)\chi(n)n^{-it}\ll_{A,B,B^{\prime}}y\log^{-A}x

for y=x1+o⁡(1)y=x^{1+o(1)}, and the claim (31) then follows from Lemma 2.2. ∎

2.5. Mean value theorems

In view of Lemma 2.4, it becomes natural to seek upper bounds on the quantity |𝒟​[f]​(12+i​t)||{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it)| for various functions ff supported on [X/C,C​X][X/C,CX]. We will primarily be interested in functions ff which are kk-divisor-bounded for some bounded kk. In such a case, we see from (23) that

∥f∥ℓ22≪kXlogOk​(1)X.\|f\|_{\ell^{2}}^{2}\ll_{k}X\log^{O_{k}(1)}X.

The heuristic of square root cancellation then suggests that the quantity |𝒟​[f]​(12+i​t)||{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it)| should be of size O⁡(Xo⁡(1))O(X^{o(1)}) for all values of tt that are of interest (except possibly for the case t=O⁡(1)t=O(1) in which there might not be sufficient oscillation). Such square root cancellation is not obtainable unconditionally with current techniques; for instance, square root cancellation for f=1(X,2​X]f=1_{(X,2X]} is equivalent to the Lindelöf hypothesis, while square root cancellation for f=Λ​1(X,2​X]f=\Lambda 1_{(X,2X]} is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis. However, we will be able to use a number of results that obtain something resembling square root cancellation on the average. The most basic instance of these results is the classical L2L^{2} mean value theorem:

Lemma 2.8 (Mean value theorem).

Suppose that f:ℕ→ℂf\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C} is supported on [X/2,4​X][X/2,4X] for some X≥2X\geq 2. Then one has

∫T0T0+T|𝒟⁡[f]​(12+i​t)|2​𝑑t≪T+XX​‖f‖ℓ22\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{0}+T}\left|{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it)\right|^{2}\ dt\ll\frac{T+X}{X}\|f\|_{\ell^{2}}^{2}

for all T>0T>0 and T0∈ℝT_{0}\in\mathbb{R}. In particular (from (23)), if ff is kk-divisor-bounded, then

∫T0T0+T|𝒟[f](12+it)|2dt≪k(T+X)logOk​(1)X.\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{0}+T}\left|{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it)\right|^{2}\ dt\ll_{k}(T+X)\log^{O_{k}(1)}X.
Proof.

See [38, Theorem 9.1]. ∎

We will need to twist Dirichlet series by Dirichlet characters. With ff as above, and any Dirichlet character χ:ℤ→ℂ\chi\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}, we can define

𝒟⁡[f]​(s,χ)≔∑nf⁡(n)ns​χ​(n){\mathcal{D}}[f](s,\chi)\coloneqq\sum_{n}\frac{f(n)}{n^{s}}\chi(n)

and more generally

𝒟⁡[f]​(s,χ,q0)≔∑nf⁡(q0​n)ns​χ​(n){\mathcal{D}}[f](s,\chi,q_{0})\coloneqq\sum_{n}\frac{f(q_{0}n)}{n^{s}}\chi(n)

for any complex ss and any natural number q0q_{0}. These Dirichlet series naturally appear when estimating Dirichlet series with a Fourier weight e⁡(a​nq)e\left(\frac{an}{q}\right), as the following simple lemma shows:

Lemma 2.9 (Expansion into Dirichlet characters).

Let f:ℕ→ℂf\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C} be a function supported on a finite set, let qq be a natural number, and let aa be coprime to qq. Let e⁡(a⋅q)e\left(\frac{a\cdot}{q}\right) denote the function n↦e⁡(a​nq)n\mapsto e\left(\frac{an}{q}\right). Then we have the pointwise bound

(33) |𝒟⁡[f​e​(a⋅q)]​(s)|≤d2​(q)q​∑q=q0​q1∑χ⁡(q1)|𝒟⁡[f]​(s,χ,q0)|\left|{\mathcal{D}}\left[fe\left(\frac{a\cdot}{q}\right)\right](s)\right|\leq\frac{d_{2}(q)}{\sqrt{q}}\sum_{q=q_{0}q_{1}}\sum_{\chi\ (q_{1})}|{\mathcal{D}}[f](s,\chi,q_{0})|

for all complex numbers ss with Re⁡(s)=12\mathrm{Re}(s)=\frac{1}{2}, where in this paper the sum ∑χ⁡(q1)\sum_{\chi\ (q_{1})} denotes a summation over all characters χ\chi (including the principal character) of period q1q_{1}, and q0,q1q_{0},q_{1} are understood to be natural numbers.

Proof.

Let ss be such that Re⁡(s)=12\mathrm{Re}(s)=\frac{1}{2}. By definition we have

𝒟⁡[f​e​(a⋅q)]​(s)=∑nf⁡(n)ns​e​(a​nq).{\mathcal{D}}\left[fe\left(\frac{a\cdot}{q}\right)\right](s)=\sum_{n}\frac{f(n)}{n^{s}}e\left(\frac{an}{q}\right).

We now decompose the nn summation in terms of the greatest common divisor q0≔(n,q)q_{0}\coloneqq(n,q) of nn and qq, obtaining (after writing q=q0​q1q=q_{0}q_{1} and n=q0​n1n=q_{0}n_{1})

𝒟[fe(a⋅q)](s)=∑q=q0​q11q0s∑n1:(n1,q1)=1f⁡(q0​n1)n1se(a​n1q1){\mathcal{D}}\left[fe\left(\frac{a\cdot}{q}\right)\right](s)=\sum_{q=q_{0}q_{1}}\frac{1}{q_{0}^{s}}\sum_{n_{1}:(n_{1},q_{1})=1}\frac{f(q_{0}n_{1})}{n_{1}^{s}}e\left(\frac{an_{1}}{q_{1}}\right)

and thus by the triangle inequality

|𝒟[fe(a⋅q)](s)|≤∑q=q0​q11q0|∑n1:(n1,q1)=1f⁡(q0​n1)n1se(a​n1q1)|.\left|{\mathcal{D}}\left[fe\left(\frac{a\cdot}{q}\right)\right](s)\right|\leq\sum_{q=q_{0}q_{1}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{q_{0}}}\left|\sum_{n_{1}:(n_{1},q_{1})=1}\frac{f(q_{0}n_{1})}{n_{1}^{s}}e\left(\frac{an_{1}}{q_{1}}\right)\right|.

Next, we perform the usual Dirichlet expansion

(34) e⁡(a​n1q1)​1(n1,q1)=1=1φ⁡(q1)​∑χ⁡(q1)χ⁡(a)​χ​(n1)​τ​(χ¯)e\left(\frac{an_{1}}{q_{1}}\right)1_{(n_{1},q_{1})=1}=\frac{1}{\varphi(q_{1})}\sum_{\chi\ (q_{1})}\chi(a)\chi(n_{1})\tau(\overline{\chi})

where τ⁡(χ¯)\tau(\overline{\chi}) is the Gauss sum

(35) τ⁡(χ¯)≔∑l=1q1e⁡(lq1)​χ⁡(l)¯\tau(\overline{\chi})\coloneqq\sum_{l=1}^{q_{1}}e\left(\frac{l}{q_{1}}\right)\overline{\chi(l)}

As is well known, we have

|τ⁡(χ¯)|≤q1|\tau(\overline{\chi})|\leq\sqrt{q_{1}}

(as can be seen for instance from making the substitution l↦a​ll\mapsto al to (35) for (a,q)=1(a,q)=1 and then applying the Parseval identity in aa). Using the crude bound

1q0​1φ⁡(q1)​q1≪1q0​d2​(q1)q1​q1≤d2​(q)q\frac{1}{\sqrt{q_{0}}}\frac{1}{\varphi(q_{1})}\sqrt{q_{1}}\ll\frac{1}{\sqrt{q_{0}}}\frac{d_{2}(q_{1})}{q_{1}}\sqrt{q_{1}}\leq\frac{d_{2}(q)}{\sqrt{q}}

and the triangle inequality, we obtain (33). ∎

It thus becomes of interest to have upper bounds, on average at least, on the quantity |𝒟⁡[f]​(12+i​t,χ,q0)||{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it,\chi,q_{0})|. We first recall a variant of Lemma 2.8, which can save a factor of q1q_{1} or so compared to that lemma when summing over characters χ\chi:

Lemma 2.10 (Mean value theorem with characters).

Suppose that f:ℕ→ℂf\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C} is supported on [X/2,4​X][X/2,4X] for some X≥2X\geq 2. Then one has

∑χ⁡(q1)∫T0T0+T|𝒟⁡[f]​(12+i​t,χ)|2≪q1​T+XX​‖f‖ℓ22​log3⁡(q1​T​X)\sum_{\chi\ (q_{1})}\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{0}+T}\left|{\mathcal{D}}[f]\left(\frac{1}{2}+it,\chi\right)\right|^{2}\ll\frac{q_{1}T+X}{X}\|f\|_{\ell^{2}}^{2}\log^{3}(q_{1}TX)

for all T≥2T\geq 2, T0∈ℝT_{0}\in\mathbb{R}, and natural numbers q1q_{1}, where χ\chi is summed over all Dirichlet characters of period q1q_{1}. In particular, if ff is kk-divisor-bounded, then (from (23)) we have

∑χ⁡(q1)∫T0T0+T|𝒟[f](12+it,χ)|2≪k(q1T+X)logOk​(1)(q1TX)\sum_{\chi\ (q_{1})}\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{0}+T}\left|{\mathcal{D}}[f]\left(\frac{1}{2}+it,\chi\right)\right|^{2}\ll_{k}(q_{1}T+X)\log^{O_{k}(1)}(q_{1}TX)
Proof.

This is a special case of [38, Theorem 9.12]. ∎

In the case when ff is an indicator function f=1[1,X]f=1_{[1,X]} we have a fourth moment estimate:

Lemma 2.11 (Fourth moment estimate).

Let X≥2X\geq 2, q1≥1q_{1}\geq 1, and T≥1T\geq 1. Let 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} be a finite set of pairs (χ,t)(\chi,t) with χ\chi a character of period qq, and t∈[−T,T]t\in[-T,T]. where δχ\delta_{\chi} is equal to 11 when χ\chi is principal, and equal to zero otherwise.

Proof.

See [2, Lemma 9]. We remark that this estimate is proven using fourth moment estimates [71] for Dirichlet LL-functions. ∎

It will be more convenient to use a (slightly weaker) integral form of this estimate:

Let X≥2X\geq 2, q1≥1q_{1}\geq 1, and T≥1T\geq 1. Then

(36) ∑χ⁡(q1)∫T/2≤|t|≤T|𝒟⁡[1[1,X]]​(12+i​t,χ)|4​𝑑t≪q1​T​(1+q12T2+X2T4)​logO⁡(1)​X.\sum_{\chi\ (q_{1})}\int_{T/2\leq|t|\leq T}\left|{\mathcal{D}}[1_{[1,X]}](\frac{1}{2}+it,\chi)\right|^{4}\ dt\ll q_{1}T\left(1+\frac{q_{1}^{2}}{T^{2}}+\frac{X^{2}}{T^{4}}\right)\log^{O(1)}X.

For each χ\chi, we cover the region T/2≤|t|≤TT/2\leq|t|\leq T by unit intervals II, and for each such II we find a point t∈It\in I that maximizes |𝒟⁡[1[1,X]]​(12+i​t,χ)||{\mathcal{D}}[1_{[1,X]}](\frac{1}{2}+it,\chi)|, then add (χ,t)(\chi,t) to 𝒮{\mathcal{S}}. Then |𝒮|≪q​T|{\mathcal{S}}|\ll qT; it is not necessarily 11-separated, but one can easily separate it into O⁡(1)O(1) 11-separated sets. Applying Lemma 2.11 (bounding δχ​(1+|t|)−4\delta_{\chi}(1+|t|)^{-4} by O⁡(1/T4)O(1/T^{4})), we obtain (36). Finally, to handle L​1[1,X]L1_{[1,X]}, one can use the integration by parts identity

and the triangle inequality (cf. Lemmas 2.1, 2.2). ∎

We will also need the following variant of the fourth moment estimate due to Jutila [40].

Proposition 2.13 (Jutila).

Let q,T≥1q,T\geq 1 and ε>0\varepsilon>0. Let T1/2+ε≪T0≪T2/3T^{1/2+\varepsilon}\ll T_{0}\ll T^{2/3} and T<t1<…<tr<2​TT<t_{1}<\ldots<t_{r}<2T with ti+1−ti>T0t_{i+1}-t_{i}>T_{0}. Then we have

See [40, Theorem 3]. This estimate is a variant of Iwaniec’s result [37] on the fourth moment of ζ\zeta in short intervals; it is however proven using a completely different and more elementary method. ∎

Using a variant of Corollary 2.5 we may truncate the Dirichlet LL-function to conclude

Let the hypotheses be as in Proposition 2.13. Then for any 1≤X≪T21\leq X\ll T^{2} and any Dirichlet character χ\chi of period qq, one has

Similarly with 1[1,X]1_{[1,X]} replaced by L​1[1,X]L1_{[1,X]}.

so by the triangle inequality again, it suffices to show that

Let tt lie in the range [T,3​T][T,3T]. From Lemma 2.4(i) with f⁡(n),σ,Tf(n),\sigma,T replaced by χ⁡(n)ni​t\frac{\chi(n)}{n^{it}}, 00, T2T^{2} respectively, we see that

whenever −T/2≤t′≤T/2-T/2\leq t^{\prime}\leq T/2. The claim (38) now follows from Fubini’s theorem. ∎

2.6. Combinatorial decompositions

We will treat the functions Λ​1(X,2​X]\Lambda 1_{(X,2X]} and dk​1(X,2​X]d_{k}1_{(X,2X]} in a unified fashion, decomposing both of these functions as certain (truncated) Dirichlet convolutions of various types, which we will call “Type djd_{j} sums” for some small j=1,2,…j=1,2,\dots and “Type II sums” respectively. More precisely, we have

Lemma 2.15 (Combinatorial decomposition).

Let k,m≥1k,m\geq 1 and 0<ε<1m0<\varepsilon<\frac{1}{m} be fixed. Let X≥2X\geq 2, and let H0H_{0} be such that X1m+ε≤H0≤XX^{\frac{1}{m}+\varepsilon}\leq H_{0}\leq X. As the name suggests, Type djd_{j} sums behave similarly to the jthj^{\operatorname{th}} divisor function djd_{j} (but with all factors in the Dirichlet convolution constrained to be supported on moderately large natural numbers). In our applications we will take mm to be at most 55, so that the only sums that appear are Type d1d_{1}, Type d2d_{2}, Type d3d_{3}, Type d4d_{4}, and Type II sums, and the dependence in the above asymptotic notation on mm can be ignored. The contributions of Type d1d_{1}, Type d2d_{2}, and Type II sums were essentially treated by previous literature; our main innovations lie in our estimation of the contributions of the Type d3d_{3} and Type d4d_{4} sums.

3. Applying the circle method

Let f,g:ℤ→ℂf,g\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} be functions supported on a finite set, and let hh be an integer. Following the Hardy-Littlewood circle method, we can express the correlation (1) as an integral

∑nf⁡(n)​g¯​(n+h)=∫𝕋Sf​(α)​Sg​(α)¯​e​(α​h)​𝑑α\sum_{n}f(n)\overline{g}(n+h)=\int_{\mathbb{T}}S_{f}(\alpha)\overline{S_{g}(\alpha)}e(\alpha h)\ d\alpha

where Sf,Sg:𝕋→ℂS_{f},S_{g}\colon\mathbb{T}\to\mathbb{C} are the exponential sums

Sf​(α)\displaystyle S_{f}(\alpha) ≔∑nf⁡(n)​e​(α​n)\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{n}f(n)e(\alpha n)
Sg​(α)\displaystyle S_{g}(\alpha) ≔∑ng⁡(n)​e​(α​n).\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{n}g(n)e(\alpha n).

If we then designate some (measurable) portion 𝔐{\mathfrak{M}} of the unit circle 𝕋\mathbb{T} to be the “major arcs”, we thus have

(52) ∑nf⁡(n)​g¯​(n+h)−MT𝔐,h=∫𝔪Sf​(α)​Sg​(α)¯​e​(α​h)​𝑑α\sum_{n}f(n)\overline{g}(n+h)-\operatorname{MT}_{{\mathfrak{M}},h}=\int_{\mathfrak{m}}S_{f}(\alpha)\overline{S_{g}(\alpha)}e(\alpha h)\ d\alpha

where MT𝔐,h\operatorname{MT}_{{\mathfrak{M}},h} is the main term

(53) MT𝔐,h≔∫𝔐Sf​(α)​Sg​(α)¯​e​(α​h)​𝑑α\operatorname{MT}_{{\mathfrak{M}},h}\coloneqq\int_{\mathfrak{M}}S_{f}(\alpha)\overline{S_{g}(\alpha)}e(\alpha h)\ d\alpha

and 𝔪≔𝕋\𝔐{\mathfrak{m}}\coloneqq\mathbb{T}\backslash{\mathfrak{M}} denotes the complementary minor arcs.

We will choose the major arcs so that the main term can be computed for any given hh by classical techniques (basically, the Siegel-Walfisz theorem, together with the analogous asymptotics for the divisor functions dkd_{k}). To control the minor arcs, we take advantage of the ability to average in hh to control this contribution by certain short L2L^{2} integrals of the exponential sum Sf​(α)S_{f}(\alpha) (the factor Sg​(α)S_{g}(\alpha) will be treated by a trivial bound).

Proposition 3.1 (Circle method).

Let H≥1H\geq 1, and let f,g,𝔐,𝔪,Sf,Sg,MT𝔐,hf,g,{\mathfrak{M}},{\mathfrak{m}},S_{f},S_{g},\operatorname{MT}_{{\mathfrak{M}},h} be as above. Then for any integer h0h_{0}, we have

From (52), the left-hand side of (54) may be written as

Next, we introduce an even non-negative Schwartz function Φ:ℝ→ℝ+\Phi\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{+} with Φ⁡(x)≥1\Phi(x)\geq 1 for all x∈[−1,1]x\in[-1,1], such that the Fourier transform Φ^​(ξ)≔∫ℝΦ⁡(x)​e​(−x​ξ)​𝑑x\hat{\Phi}(\xi)\coloneqq\int_{\mathbb{R}}\Phi(x)e(-x\xi)\ dx is supported in [−1/2,1/2][-1/2,1/2]. (Such a function may be constructed by starting with the inverse Fourier transform of an even test function supported on a small neighbourhood of the origin, and then squaring.) Then we may bound the preceding expression by

Expanding out the square, rearranging, and using the triangle inequality, we may bound this expression by

From the Poisson summation formula we have

where α~,β~\tilde{\alpha},\tilde{\beta} are any lifts of α,β\alpha,\beta from 𝕋\mathbb{T} to ℝ\mathbb{R}. In particular, this expression is of size O⁡(H)O(H), and vanishes unless β\beta lies in the interval [α−1/2​H,α+1/2​H][\alpha-1/2H,\alpha+1/2H]. Shifting hh by h0h_{0}, the claim follows. ∎

From the Plancherel identities

and so the right-hand side of (54) may be crudely upper bounded by H​‖f‖ℓ22​‖g‖ℓ22H\|f\|_{\ell^{2}}^{2}\|g\|_{\ell^{2}}^{2}, which is essentially the trivial bound on (54) that one obtains from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Thus, any significant improvement (e.g. by a large power of log⁡X\log X) over (58) for minor arc α\alpha will lead to an approximation of the form

∑nf⁡(n)​g⁡(n+h)¯≈MTℳ,h\sum_{n}f(n)\overline{g(n+h)}\approx\operatorname{MT}_{{\mathcal{M}},h}

for most h∈[h0−H,h0+H]h\in[h_{0}-H,h_{0}+H]. We formalize this argument as follows:

Let H≥1H\geq 1 and η,F,G,X>0\eta,F,G,X>0. Remark 3.5.

The bound (63) is being used here to establish Theorem 1.3. In the converse direction, it is possible to use Theorem 1.3 to establish (63); we sketch the argument as follows. The left-hand side of (63) may be bounded by

∫ℝ|Sf​(θ)|2​η​(Xσ+ε​(θ−aq−β))​𝑑θ\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left|S_{f}\left(\theta\right)\right|^{2}\eta\left(X^{\sigma+\varepsilon}\left(\theta-\frac{a}{q}-\beta\right)\right)\ d\theta

The inner sum can be controlled for most hh using Theorem 1.3, and the contribution of the exceptional values of hh can be controlled by upper bound sieves. We leave the details to the interested reader.

5. Reduction to a Dirichlet series mean value estimate

We begin the proof of Proposition 3.4. As discussed in the introduction, we will estimate the expressions (63), (62), which currently involve the additive frequency variable α\alpha, by expressions involving the multiplicative frequency tt, by performing a sequence of Fourier-analytic transformations and changes of variable.

The starting point will be the following treatment of the q=1q=1 case:

and so from the L2L^{2} mean value estimate (Lemma 2.8) we see that for ff a kk-divisor bounded function (70) trivially implies the bound

Appendix A Mean value estimate

In this section we prove Proposition 5.5. This estimate is fairly standard, for instance following from the methods in [25, Chapter 9]; for the convenience of the reader we sketch a full proof here.

Let ε,A,B,X,q0,q1,f,B′\varepsilon,A,B,X,q_{0},q_{1},f,B^{\prime} be as in Proposition 5.5. We first invoke Lemma 2.16 with m=3m=3, and with ε\varepsilon and HH replaced by ε/10\varepsilon/10 and X1/3+ε/10X^{1/3+\varepsilon/10} respectively. We conclude that the function (χ,t)↦𝒟⁡[f]​(12+i​t,χ,q0)(\chi,t)\mapsto{\mathcal{D}}[f](\frac{1}{2}+it,\chi,q_{0}) can be decomposed as a linear combination (with coefficients of size Ok,ε​(d2​(q0)Ok,ε​(1))O_{k,\varepsilon}(d_{2}(q_{0})^{O_{k,\varepsilon}(1)})) of Ok,ε​(logOk,ε​(1)⁡X)O_{k,\varepsilon}(\log^{O_{k,\varepsilon}(1)}X) functions of the form (χ,t)↦𝒟⁡[f~]​(12+i​t,χ)(\chi,t)\mapsto{\mathcal{D}}[\tilde{f}](\frac{1}{2}+it,\chi), where f~:ℕ→ℂ\tilde{f}\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C} is one of the following forms:

  • (Type d1d_{1}, d2d_{2} sum)

    A function of the form

    (119) f~=(α∗β1∗⋯∗βj)​1(X/q0,2​X/q0]\tilde{f}=(\alpha\ast\beta_{1}\ast\dots\ast\beta_{j})1_{(X/q_{0},2X/q_{0}]}

    for some arithmetic functions α,β1,…,βj:ℕ→ℂ\alpha,\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{j}\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C}, where j=1,2j=1,2, α\alpha is Ok,ε​(1)O_{k,\varepsilon}(1)-divisor-bounded and supported on [N,2​N][N,2N], and each βi\beta_{i}, i=1,…,ji=1,\dots,j is either of the form βi=1(Mi,2​Mi]\beta_{i}=1_{(M_{i},2M_{i}]} or βi=L​1(Mi,2​Mi]\beta_{i}=L1_{(M_{i},2M_{i}]} for some N,M1,…,MjN,M_{1},\dots,M_{j} obeying the bounds

    1≪N≪k,εXε/10,1\ll N\ll_{k,\varepsilon}X^{\varepsilon/10},
    NM1…Mj≍k,εX/q0,NM_{1}\dots M_{j}\asymp_{k,\varepsilon}X/q_{0},

    and

    X1/3+ε/10≪M1≪⋯≪Mj≪X/q0.X^{1/3+\varepsilon/10}\ll M_{1}\ll\dots\ll M_{j}\ll X/q_{0}.
  • (Type II sum)

    A function of the form

    f~=(α∗β)​1(X/q0,2​X/q0]\tilde{f}=(\alpha\ast\beta)1_{(X/q_{0},2X/q_{0}]}

    for some Ok,ε​(1)O_{k,\varepsilon}(1)-divisor-bounded arithmetic functions α,β:ℕ→ℂ\alpha,\beta\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C} with good cancellation supported on [N,2​N][N,2N] and [M,2​M][M,2M] respectively, for some N,MN,M obeying the bounds

    Xε/10≪N≪X1/3+ε/10X^{\varepsilon/10}\ll N\ll X^{1/3+\varepsilon/10}

    and

    NM≍k,εX/q0.NM\asymp_{k,\varepsilon}X/q_{0}.

    The good cancellation bounds (29) are permitted to depend on the parameter BB appearing in the bound q0≤logB⁡Xq_{0}\leq\log^{B}X.

  • (Small sum)

    A function f~\tilde{f} supported on (X/q0,2​X/q0](X/q_{0},2X/q_{0}] obeying the bound

    (120) ∥f~∥ℓ22≪k,εX1−ε/80.\|\tilde{f}\|_{\ell^{2}}^{2}\ll_{k,\varepsilon}X^{1-\varepsilon/80}.

By the L2L^{2} triangle inequality (and enlarging AA as necessary), it thus suffices to establish the bound

(121) ∫logB′⁡X≤|t|≤X5/6−ε|𝒟[f~](12+it′,χ,q0)|2dt′≪k,ε,A,B,B′Xlog−AX.\int_{\log^{B^{\prime}}X\leq|t|\leq X^{5/6-\varepsilon}}\left|{\mathcal{D}}[\tilde{f}]\left(\frac{1}{2}+it^{\prime},\chi,q_{0}\right)\right|^{2}\ dt^{\prime}\ll_{k,\varepsilon,A,B,B^{\prime}}X\log^{-A}X.

for each individual character χ\chi and f~\tilde{f} one of the above forms.

We first dispose of the small sum case. From Lemma 2.8 and (120) we have

∫|t|≤X5/6−ε|𝒟[f~](12+it,χ)|2dt≪kX1−ε/80logOk​(1)X.\int_{|t|\leq X^{5/6-\varepsilon}}\left|{\mathcal{D}}[\tilde{f}]\left(\frac{1}{2}+it,\chi\right)\right|^{2}\ dt\ll_{k}X^{1-\varepsilon/80}\log^{O_{k}(1)}X.

which gives (121) (with a power savings).

In the remaining Type d1d_{1}, Type d2d_{2}, and Type II cases, f~\tilde{f} is of the form f~=f′​1(X/q0,2​X/q0]\tilde{f}=f^{\prime}1_{(X/q_{0},2X/q_{0}]}, where f′f^{\prime} is of the form α∗β1\alpha\ast\beta_{1}, α∗β1∗β2\alpha\ast\beta_{1}\ast\beta_{2}, or α∗β\alpha\ast\beta in the Type d1d_{1}, Type d2d_{2}, and Type II cases respectively. From Corollary 2.5 one has

|𝒟⁡[f~]​(12+i​t,χ)|≪∫|u|≤X5/6−ε|𝒟⁡[f′]​(12+i​t+i​u,χ)|​d​u1+|u|+1.|{\mathcal{D}}[\tilde{f}](\frac{1}{2}+it,\chi)|\ll\int_{|u|\leq X^{5/6-\varepsilon}}\left|{\mathcal{D}}[f^{\prime}]\left(\frac{1}{2}+it+iu,\chi\right)\right|\frac{du}{1+|u|}+1.
